title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Expenses of the Sovereign or Commonwealth
Part I: The Expense of Defence

The sovereign's first duty is to protect society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies, and this can be done only with a military force. But the cost of building that force in peacetime and of using it in wartime varies enormously from one stage of society to another, and from one period of development to the next.

Take nations of hunters first, the lowest and crudest stage of society, as we see it among the native tribes of North America. There, every man is a warrior as well as a hunter. When he goes to war, whether to defend his society or to avenge wrongs done to it by others, he supports himself by his own labour, exactly as he does when he is at home. His society bears no expense at all, neither to prepare him for the field nor to keep him there while he serves. (In this stage of things there is, strictly speaking, neither a sovereign nor a commonwealth.)

Nations of shepherds stand at a more advanced stage, as we find among the Tartars and the Arabs, and here too every man is a warrior. Such peoples usually have no fixed home but live in tents or in a kind of covered wagon that can be moved easily from place to place. The whole tribe or nation shifts its location with the seasons and with whatever else happens to drive it. Once its herds and flocks have eaten the forage in one part of the country, it moves to a second, and then to a third. In the dry season it comes down to the riverbanks; in the wet season it withdraws to the higher ground. When such a nation goes to war, the warriors will not leave their herds and flocks to the weak protection of their old men, women, and children, and these in turn cannot be left behind without protection or food. The whole nation, used to a wandering life even in peacetime, can take the field easily in war. Whether it marches as an army or moves about as a band of herdsmen, the way of life is much the same, though the purpose is very different. So they all go to war together, and each does as well as he can. Among the Tartars, even the women have often been known to fight. If they win, everything that belongs to the enemy tribe is the prize of victory; if they lose, everything is lost, and not only their herds and flocks but their women and children become the conqueror's spoils. Even most of those who survive the battle are forced to submit to him simply to stay alive. The rest are usually scattered and lost in the desert.

The everyday life and everyday activity of a Tartar or Arab prepare him well enough for war. Running, wrestling, playing at cudgels, throwing the javelin, drawing the bow, and the like are the common pastimes of people who live in the open air, and all of them mirror the actions of war. When a Tartar or Arab actually goes to war, he is supported by his own herds and flocks, which he brings along with him, just as in peacetime. His chief or sovereign (and these nations all have chiefs or sovereigns) spends nothing to prepare him for the field, and once he is there, the prospect of plunder is the only pay he expects or asks for.

An army of hunters can rarely exceed two or three hundred men. The unreliable food supply that hunting provides could seldom let a larger number stay together for any length of time. An army of shepherds, by contrast, may sometimes reach two or three hundred thousand. As long as nothing blocks their advance, as long as they can keep moving from one district whose forage they have used up to another that is still untouched, there seems to be almost no limit to how many can march together. A nation of hunters can never threaten the civilized nations near it; a nation of shepherds can. Nothing is more contemptible than an Indian war in North America; nothing, on the other hand, is more terrifying than the Tartar invasions that have so often struck Asia. Thucydides judged that neither Europe nor Asia could resist the Scythians if they united, and the experience of every age has borne this out. The peoples of the vast but defenceless plains of Scythia or Tartary have often been brought together under the rule of some conquering horde's or clan's chief, and their union has always been marked by the havoc and devastation of Asia. The peoples of the inhospitable deserts of Arabia, the other great shepherd nation, have been united only once, under Muhammad and his immediate successors. Their union, which owed more to religious zeal than to conquest, was marked in the same way. If the hunting nations of America ever became shepherds, their nearness would be far more dangerous to the European colonies than it is now.

At a still more advanced stage of society we reach the farming nations that have little foreign trade and no manufactures beyond the coarse household goods that nearly every family makes for its own use. Here too every man is either a warrior or easily becomes one. People who live by agriculture generally spend the whole day outdoors, exposed to every kind of weather. The toughness of their ordinary life prepares them for the hardships of war, some of which closely resemble their everyday work. The labour of a ditch-digger prepares him to dig trenches and fortify a camp just as it prepares him to enclose a field. The usual pastimes of such farmers are the same as those of shepherds and likewise mirror the actions of war. But because farmers have less spare time than shepherds, they take part in those pastimes less often. They are soldiers, but soldiers who are not quite so practised in their drill. Still, such as they are, it rarely costs the sovereign or commonwealth anything to prepare them for the field.

Agriculture, even at its crudest and lowest, assumes a settlement, some kind of fixed home that cannot be abandoned without heavy loss. So when a nation of plain farmers goes to war, the whole people cannot take the field at once. At the very least, the old men, women, and children must stay home to look after the dwellings. But all the men of military age can take the field, and in small nations of this kind they have often done so. In every nation, the men of military age are reckoned at about a fourth or a fifth of the whole population. If the campaign begins after sowing and ends before harvest, both the farmer and his main labourers can be spared from the farm without much loss. He trusts that the work needed in the meantime can be done well enough by the old men, women, and children. So he is willing to serve without pay during a short campaign, and it often costs the sovereign or commonwealth as little to keep him in the field as to prepare him for it. The citizens of all the various states of ancient Greece seem to have served this way until after the second Persian war, and the people of the Peloponnese until after the Peloponnesian war. Thucydides notes that the Peloponnesians generally left the field in summer and went home to bring in the harvest. The Roman people, under their kings and during the early ages of the republic, served the same way. It was not until the siege of Veii that those who stayed home began to contribute something toward supporting those who went to war. In the European monarchies built on the ruins of the Roman empire, both before and for some time after the establishment of what is properly called feudal law, the great lords and all their immediate dependents used to serve the crown at their own expense. In the field, just as at home, they supported themselves from their own income, not from any stipend or pay handed to them by the king for that particular occasion.

At a more advanced stage of society, two different causes make it altogether impossible for those who take the field to support themselves at their own expense: the growth of manufactures, and improvements in the art of war.

Even if a farmer joins an expedition, as long as it begins after sowing and ends before harvest, the interruption of his work will not always cut his income much. Without his labour, Nature does most of the remaining work herself. But the moment a craftsman, a smith, a carpenter, or a weaver, say, leaves his workshop, the only source of his income dries up completely. Nature does nothing for him; he does everything for himself. So when he takes the field to defend the public, having no income to live on, he must necessarily be supported by the public. And in a country where a large part of the population are craftsmen and manufacturers, a large part of those who go to war must come from those classes, and so must be supported by the public for as long as they serve it.

And once the art of war has gradually grown into a very intricate and complicated science, once the outcome of war is no longer settled, as in the first ages of society, by a single disorderly skirmish or battle, but the contest is usually drawn out over several different campaigns, each lasting most of the year, then it becomes universally necessary for the public to support those who serve it in war, at least while they are so employed. Whatever such men might ordinarily do in peacetime, a service so long and so costly would otherwise be far too heavy a burden on them. Accordingly, after the second Persian war the armies of Athens seem to have been made up generally of mercenary troops, partly citizens, it is true, but partly foreigners as well, and all of them equally hired and paid at the state's expense. From the time of the siege of Veii, the armies of Rome received pay for their service for as long as they stayed in the field. Under feudal governments, the military service of both the great lords and their immediate dependents was, after a certain point, universally exchanged for a money payment, which was used to support those who served in their place.

The number who can go to war, in proportion to the whole population, is necessarily much smaller in a civilized than in a crude state of society. In a civilized society, since the soldiers are supported entirely by the labour of those who are not soldiers, their number can never exceed what the rest can support, on top of supporting, in a manner suited to their stations, both themselves and the other officers of government and law whom they must also maintain. In the small farming states of ancient Greece, a fourth or a fifth of the whole population regarded themselves as soldiers, and would sometimes, it is said, take the field. Among the civilized nations of modern Europe, the usual estimate is that no more than a hundredth of any country's people can be employed as soldiers without ruining the country that pays for their service.

The expense of preparing the army for the field does not seem to have become significant in any nation until long after the cost of maintaining it in the field had fallen entirely on the sovereign or commonwealth. In all the various republics of ancient Greece, learning one's military drill was a necessary part of the education that the state required of every free citizen. In every city there seems to have been a public field where, under the protection of the public magistrate, the young were taught their various exercises by various masters. This very simple arrangement was the whole expense any Greek state seems ever to have borne in preparing its citizens for war. In ancient Rome, the exercises of the Campus Martius served the same purpose as those of the Gymnasium in ancient Greece. Under feudal governments, the many public ordinances requiring the citizens of every district to practise archery and several other military exercises were meant to serve the same purpose, but do not seem to have served it nearly so well. Whether from the indifference of the officers charged with enforcing them, or from some other cause, they appear to have been universally neglected, and as all those governments developed, military exercises seem to have gradually fallen out of use among the great body of the people.

In the republics of ancient Greece and Rome, throughout their existence, and under feudal governments for a considerable time after they were first set up, the trade of a soldier was not a separate, distinct trade that formed the sole or principal occupation of any particular class of citizens. Every subject of the state, whatever the ordinary trade or occupation by which he made his living, regarded himself as fit, on all ordinary occasions, to act as a soldier as well, and on many extraordinary occasions as bound to do so.

The art of war, however, is surely the noblest of all the arts, and as improvement advances it necessarily becomes one of the most complicated among them. The state of the mechanical arts, and of certain other arts to which it is necessarily linked, sets the degree of perfection it can reach at any given time. But to carry it to that degree of perfection, it must become the sole or principal occupation of a particular class of citizens; and the division of labour is as necessary to improving this art as to improving every other. In other arts, the division of labour is naturally introduced by the foresight of individuals, who find they serve their own interest better by sticking to one trade than by practising many. But only the wisdom of the state can make the trade of a soldier a particular trade, separate and distinct from all others. A private citizen who, in a time of deep peace and with no particular encouragement from the public, spent most of his time on military exercises might no doubt improve himself greatly in them and enjoy himself very well, but he certainly would not be serving his own interest. Only the wisdom of the state can make it worth his while to give up most of his time to this peculiar occupation; and states have not always had this wisdom, even when their circumstances had reached the point where their very survival required it.

A shepherd has a great deal of leisure; a farmer, at the crude stage of farming, has some; a craftsman or manufacturer has none at all. The first can spend a great deal of his time on martial exercises without any loss; the second can spend some of it; but the last cannot spend a single hour on them without some loss, and concern for his own interest naturally leads him to neglect them entirely. The improvements in farming that the progress of arts and manufactures inevitably brings leave the farmer with as little leisure as the craftsman. Military exercises come to be neglected by the country people as much as by the townspeople, and the great body of the people becomes wholly unwarlike. At the same time, the wealth that always follows improvements in agriculture and manufactures, and that is really nothing more than the accumulated product of those improvements, tempts all their neighbours to invade. An industrious, and therefore wealthy, nation is of all nations the most likely to be attacked; and unless the state takes some new measure for the public defence, the people's natural habits leave them altogether unable to defend themselves.
In these circumstances, there seem to be only two ways for the state to make any decent provision for the public defence.

It may, first, by means of a very strict regulation, and against the whole bent of the people's interest, talents, and inclinations, enforce the practice of military exercises and oblige either all citizens of military age, or a certain number of them, to add the trade of a soldier to whatever other trade or profession they happen to follow.

Or, secondly, by maintaining and employing a certain number of citizens in the constant practice of military exercises, it may make the trade of a soldier a particular trade, separate and distinct from all others.

If the state takes the first of these two paths, its military force is said to be a militia; if the second, a standing army. For the soldiers of a standing army, practising military exercises is their sole or principal occupation, and the support or pay the state gives them is their main and ordinary means of living. For the soldiers of a militia, practising military exercises is only an occasional activity, and they get their main and ordinary means of living from some other occupation. In a militia, the character of the labourer, craftsman, or tradesman dominates over that of the soldier; in a standing army, the character of the soldier dominates over every other; and this distinction seems to be the essential difference between these two kinds of military force.

Militias have come in several different forms. In some countries, the citizens meant to defend the state seem to have been only exercised, without being, so to speak, regimented, that is, without being divided into separate, distinct bodies of troops, each drilling under its own proper and permanent officers. In the republics of ancient Greece and Rome, each citizen, as long as he stayed home, seems to have practised his exercises either on his own or with whichever of his equals he liked best, and not to have been attached to any particular body of troops until he was actually called up to take the field. In other countries, the militia has not only been exercised but regimented. In England, in Switzerland, and, I believe, in every other country of modern Europe where any imperfect military force of this kind has been set up, every militiaman, even in peacetime, is attached to a particular body of troops that drills under its own proper and permanent officers.

Before the invention of firearms, the superior army was the one whose soldiers each had the greatest individual skill and dexterity in handling their weapons. Bodily strength and agility mattered enormously and usually decided the outcome of battles. But this skill and dexterity could be acquired only the way fencing is today, by practising not in large bodies but each man separately, in a particular school, under a particular master, or with his own equals and companions. Since the invention of firearms, bodily strength and agility, or even extraordinary skill and dexterity with weapons, though far from worthless, count for less. The nature of the weapon, while it by no means puts the clumsy man on a level with the skilful, puts him closer to that level than he ever was before. All the dexterity and skill needed to use it, it is supposed, can be acquired well enough by practising in large bodies.

Regularity, order, and prompt obedience to command are qualities that, in modern armies, do more to decide the outcome of battles than the soldiers' dexterity and skill with their weapons. But the noise of firearms, the smoke, and the unseen death to which every man feels himself exposed at every moment, the instant he comes within cannon-shot and often long before the battle can properly be said to have begun, must make it very hard to keep up any real degree of this regularity, order, and prompt obedience, even at the very start of a modern battle. In an ancient battle there was no noise but the human voice, no smoke, and no unseen cause of wounds or death. Every man, until some deadly weapon actually came near him, could see clearly that no such weapon was close. In these conditions, and among troops who had some confidence in their own skill and dexterity with their weapons, it must have been a good deal easier to keep some degree of regularity and order, not only at the start but throughout the whole course of an ancient battle, until one of the two armies was fairly beaten. But the habits of regularity, order, and prompt obedience to command can be acquired only by troops drilled in large bodies.
A militia, however it may be disciplined or exercised, must always be far inferior to a well-disciplined and well-exercised standing army.

Soldiers who drill only once a week, or once a month, can never become as expert with their weapons as those who drill every day, or every other day. And though this may matter less in modern times than it did in ancient times, the acknowledged superiority of the Prussian troops, owing, it is said, very much to their greater skill in drill, may convince us that even today it still matters a great deal.

Soldiers who are bound to obey their officer only once a week, or once a month, and who at all other times are free to run their own affairs in their own way, answerable to him in no respect, can never feel the same awe in his presence or the same readiness to obey as those whose whole life and conduct he directs every day, who even rise and go to bed, or at least retire to quarters, on his orders. In what is called discipline, or the habit of ready obedience, a militia must always fall still further short of a standing army than it sometimes does in what is called the manual exercise, the handling and use of weapons. And in modern war, the habit of ready and instant obedience matters far more than a considerable superiority in handling weapons.

The militias that are best are those which, like the Tartar or Arab militia, go to war under the same chieftains they are used to obeying in peace. In their respect for their officers and their habit of ready obedience, they come closest to standing armies. The Highland militia, when it served under its own chieftains, had some advantage of the same kind. But because the Highlanders were stationary rather than wandering shepherds, having all a fixed home and not being used in peacetime to follow their chieftain from place to place, in wartime they were less willing to follow him any great distance or to stay long in the field. Once they had taken any booty they were eager to go home, and his authority was seldom enough to keep them. In obedience they were always far below what is reported of the Tartars and Arabs. And because their settled life kept them indoors more, the Highlanders were always less used to military exercises and less expert with their weapons than the Tartars and Arabs are said to be.

It must be noted, however, that a militia of any kind that has served several campaigns in a row in the field becomes in every respect a standing army. The soldiers drill with their weapons every day, and being constantly under their officers' command, they grow used to the same prompt obedience found in standing armies. What they were before they took the field hardly matters. After a few campaigns they necessarily become in every respect a standing army. Should the war in America drag on through another campaign, the American militia may become in every respect a match for that standing army whose valour appeared, in the last war at least, to be no less than that of the toughest veterans of France and Spain.
Once this distinction is well understood, the history of every age will be found to bear witness to the irresistible superiority that a well-regulated standing army has over a militia.

One of the first standing armies of which we have any clear account in well-attested history is that of Philip of Macedon. His frequent wars with the Thracians, Illyrians, Thessalians, and some of the Greek cities near Macedon gradually shaped his troops, which were probably a militia at first, into the exact discipline of a standing army. When he was at peace, which he rarely was, and never for long at a stretch, he was careful not to disband that army. After a long and violent struggle it beat and subdued the brave, well-exercised militias of the chief republics of ancient Greece, and afterwards, with very little struggle, the soft and poorly exercised militia of the great Persian empire. The fall of the Greek republics and of the Persian empire was the result of the irresistible superiority that a standing army has over every other kind of militia. It is the first great revolution in the affairs of mankind of which history has preserved any clear and detailed account.
The fall of Carthage and the consequent rise of Rome is the second. All the shifts in the fortunes of those two famous republics can be very well explained by the same cause.

From the end of the first to the beginning of the second Punic war, the armies of Carthage were continually in the field, serving under three great generals who succeeded one another in command: Hamilcar, his son-in-law Hasdrubal, and his son Hannibal. They were employed first in punishing their own rebellious slaves, then in subduing the revolted nations of Africa, and finally in conquering the great kingdom of Spain. The army that Hannibal led from Spain into Italy must, through those various wars, have been gradually shaped into the exact discipline of a standing army. The Romans, meanwhile, though not entirely at peace, had not during this period been engaged in any war of great consequence, and their military discipline, it is generally said, had grown a good deal slack. The Roman armies that Hannibal met at the Trebia, at Lake Trasimene, and at Cannae were militias facing a standing army. This circumstance probably did more than anything else to decide the outcome of those battles.

The standing army that Hannibal left behind him in Spain had the same superiority over the militia the Romans sent to oppose it, and within a few years, under the command of his brother, the younger Hasdrubal, it drove them almost entirely out of that country.

Hannibal was poorly supplied from home. The Roman militia, being continually in the field, became as the war went on a well-disciplined and well-exercised standing army, and Hannibal's superiority shrank day by day. Hasdrubal judged it necessary to lead the whole, or nearly the whole, of the standing army he commanded in Spain to his brother's aid in Italy. On this march he is said to have been misled by his guides, and in a country he did not know he was surprised and attacked by another standing army, in every respect equal or superior to his own, and was completely defeated.

Once Hasdrubal had left Spain, the great Scipio found nothing to oppose him there but a militia inferior to his own. He conquered and subdued that militia, and in the course of the war his own militia necessarily became a well-disciplined and well-exercised standing army. That standing army was afterwards carried over to Africa, where it found nothing but a militia to oppose it. To defend Carthage it became necessary to recall Hannibal's standing army. The disheartened and often-beaten African militia joined it, and at the battle of Zama made up the greater part of Hannibal's troops. The outcome of that day decided the fate of the two rival republics.

From the end of the second Punic war to the fall of the Roman republic, the armies of Rome were in every respect standing armies. The standing army of Macedon put up some resistance to their arms. At the height of their greatness it cost the Romans two great wars and three great battles to subdue that little kingdom, whose conquest would probably have been still harder but for the cowardice of its last king. The militias of all the civilized nations of the ancient world, of Greece, of Syria, and of Egypt, offered only a feeble resistance to the standing armies of Rome. The militias of some barbarous nations defended themselves much better. The Scythian or Tartar militia, which Mithridates drew from the countries north of the Black and Caspian seas, was the most formidable enemy the Romans had to face after the second Punic war. The Parthian and German militias, too, were always respectable and on several occasions won very considerable advantages over the Roman armies. In general, however, when the Roman armies were well led, they appear to have been very much superior; and if the Romans did not pursue the final conquest of either Parthia or Germany, it was probably because they judged it not worth adding those two barbarous countries to an empire that was already too large. The ancient Parthians appear to have been a nation of Scythian or Tartar descent who always kept a good deal of their ancestors' manners. The ancient Germans, like the Scythians or Tartars, were a nation of wandering shepherds who went to war under the same chiefs they were used to following in peace. Their militia was exactly the same kind as that of the Scythians or Tartars, from whom they too were probably descended.

Many different causes combined to relax the discipline of the Roman armies. Its extreme severity was perhaps one of them. In the days of their greatness, when no enemy seemed able to face them, their heavy armour was laid aside as a needless burden and their hard exercises neglected as needlessly toilsome. Under the Roman emperors, moreover, the standing armies of Rome, especially those guarding the German and Pannonian frontiers, became dangerous to their own masters, against whom they often set up their own generals. To make them less formidable, some authors say Diocletian, others Constantine, first pulled them back from the frontier, where they had always before been encamped in large bodies, generally of two or three legions each, and scattered them in small bodies through the various provincial towns, from which they were hardly ever moved except when it became necessary to repel an invasion. Small bodies of soldiers, quartered in trading and manufacturing towns and seldom moved from those quarters, became tradesmen, craftsmen, and manufacturers themselves. The civilian character came to dominate over the military, and the standing armies of Rome gradually degenerated into a corrupt, neglected, and undisciplined militia, unable to resist the attack of the German and Scythian militias that soon afterwards invaded the western empire. Only by hiring the militia of some of those nations to oppose the militia of others were the emperors able to defend themselves for a time. The fall of the western empire is the third great revolution in the affairs of mankind of which ancient history has preserved any clear or detailed account. It was brought about by the irresistible superiority that the militia of a barbarous nation has over that of a civilized one, that the militia of a nation of shepherds has over that of a nation of farmers, craftsmen, and manufacturers. The victories won by militias have generally been not over standing armies but over other militias inferior to them in exercise and discipline. Such were the victories the Greek militia won over that of the Persian empire, and such too were those that, in later times, the Swiss militia won over that of the Austrians and Burgundians.

The military force of the German and Scythian nations who settled themselves on the ruins of the western empire stayed for a time the same kind it had been in their original country. It was a militia of shepherds and farmers that in wartime took the field under the same chieftains it was used to obeying in peace. So it was tolerably well exercised and tolerably well disciplined. As arts and industry advanced, however, the chieftains' authority gradually decayed, and the great body of the people had less time to spare for military exercises. Both the discipline and the exercise of the feudal militia therefore gradually fell into ruin, and standing armies were gradually introduced to take its place. And once the expedient of a standing army had been adopted by one civilized nation, all its neighbours necessarily had to follow suit. They soon found that their safety depended on it, and that their own militia was altogether unable to resist the attack of such an army.

The soldiers of a standing army, though they may never have seen an enemy, have frequently shown all the courage of veteran troops and, the very moment they took the field, proved fit to face the toughest and most experienced veterans. In 1756, when the Russian army marched into Poland, the valour of the Russian soldiers did not appear inferior to that of the Prussians, then supposed to be the toughest and most experienced veterans in Europe. Yet the Russian empire had enjoyed deep peace for nearly twenty years before, and could at that time have had very few soldiers who had ever seen an enemy. When the Spanish war broke out in 1739, England had enjoyed deep peace for about twenty-eight years. Yet the valour of her soldiers, far from being spoiled by that long peace, was never more conspicuous than in the attempt on Cartagena, the first unfortunate exploit of that unfortunate war. In a long peace the generals may sometimes lose their skill; but where a well-regulated standing army has been kept up, the soldiers never seem to lose their valour.

When a civilized nation depends for its defence on a militia, it is always at risk of being conquered by any barbarous nation that happens to be its neighbour. The frequent conquests of all the civilized countries of Asia by the Tartars sufficiently prove the natural superiority that the militia of a barbarous nation has over that of a civilized one. A well-regulated standing army is superior to every militia. Such an army, since it can best be maintained by a rich and civilized nation, is also the only thing that can defend such a nation against the invasion of a poor and barbarous neighbour. It is only by means of a standing army, then, that the civilization of any country can be perpetuated, or even preserved, for any length of time.

Just as a civilized country can be defended only by means of a well-regulated standing army, so it is only by such an army that a barbarous country can be quickly and tolerably civilized. A standing army imposes the sovereign's law with irresistible force throughout the remotest provinces of the empire and keeps up some degree of regular government in countries that could otherwise admit of none. Whoever examines closely the improvements that Peter the Great introduced into the Russian empire will find that they almost all come down to the establishment of a well-regulated standing army. It is the instrument that carries out and maintains all his other measures. The degree of order and internal peace that empire has enjoyed ever since is owing entirely to the influence of that army.

Men of republican principles have been suspicious of a standing army as a danger to liberty. And it certainly is dangerous wherever the interest of the general and of the chief officers is not necessarily bound up with supporting the constitution of the state. Caesar's standing army destroyed the Roman republic. Cromwell's standing army turned the Long Parliament out of doors. But where the sovereign is himself the general, and the chief nobility and gentry of the country are the chief officers of the army, where the military force is placed under the command of those who have the greatest interest in supporting the civil authority because they hold the greatest share of it, a standing army can never be dangerous to liberty. On the contrary, it may in some cases be favourable to liberty. The security it gives the sovereign makes unnecessary that troublesome suspicion which, in some modern republics, seems to watch over the smallest actions and to be forever ready to disturb the peace of every citizen. Where the magistrate's security, even when backed by the leading people of the country, is endangered by every popular discontent, where a small disturbance can in a few hours bring about a great revolution, the whole authority of government must be used to suppress and punish every murmur and complaint against it. A sovereign, by contrast, who feels himself supported not only by the natural aristocracy of the country but by a well-regulated standing army, can be little troubled by the rudest, most groundless, and most licentious protests. He can safely pardon or ignore them, and his sense of his own superiority naturally inclines him to do so. That degree of liberty which verges on licence can be tolerated only in countries where the sovereign is secured by a well-regulated standing army. It is only in such countries that public safety does not require the sovereign to be trusted with any discretionary power to suppress even the impertinent excesses of this licentious liberty.

The sovereign's first duty, then, that of defending society from the violence and injustice of other independent societies, grows steadily more and more expensive as society advances in civilization. The military force of the society, which originally cost the sovereign nothing in peace or in war, must, as improvement advances, first be maintained by him in wartime and afterwards even in peacetime.

The great change brought into the art of war by the invention of firearms has driven up still further both the cost of exercising and disciplining any given number of soldiers in peacetime and the cost of employing them in war. Both their weapons and their ammunition have grown more expensive. A musket is a costlier machine than a javelin or a bow and arrows; a cannon or a mortar, than a ballista or a catapult. The powder spent in a modern review is lost beyond recovery and costs a great deal. The javelins and arrows thrown or shot in an ancient one could easily be picked up again and were, besides, of very little value. The cannon and the mortar are not only much dearer but much heavier machines than the ballista or catapult, and cost more not only to prepare for the field but to transport to it. And because modern artillery is so very superior to that of the ancients, it has become much harder, and so much more expensive, to fortify a town so that it can resist, even for a few weeks, the attack of that superior artillery. In modern times many different causes combine to make the defence of society more expensive. The unavoidable effects of the natural progress of improvement have, in this respect, been considerably heightened by a great revolution in the art of war, which a mere accident, the invention of gunpowder, seems to have brought about.

In modern war, the great cost of firearms gives a clear advantage to the nation best able to bear that cost, and so to a rich and civilized nation over a poor and barbarous one. In ancient times the rich and civilized found it hard to defend themselves against the poor and barbarous. In modern times the poor and barbarous find it hard to defend themselves against the rich and civilized. The invention of firearms, which at first sight seems so destructive, is certainly favourable both to the permanence and to the spread of civilization.
Part II: The Expense of Justice

The sovereign's second duty, that of protecting, as far as possible, every member of society from the injustice or oppression of every other member, in other words the duty of administering justice precisely, calls for two very different levels of expense in the different periods of society.

Among nations of hunters, since there is scarcely any property, or at least none worth more than two or three days' labour, there is seldom any established magistrate or any regular administration of justice. Men who have no property can harm one another only in their persons or their reputations. But when one man kills, wounds, beats, or slanders another, though the victim suffers, the man who does it gains nothing. It is otherwise with injuries to property. There the gain of the man who does the injury is often equal to the loss of the man who suffers it. Envy, malice, or resentment are the only passions that can drive one man to injure another in his person or reputation. But most men are not very often under the sway of those passions, and the very worst are so only now and then. And since indulging them, however agreeable it may be to certain characters, brings no real or lasting advantage, in most men it is usually held in check by prudent considerations. Men can live together in society with some tolerable degree of security even where there is no civil magistrate to protect them from the injustice of those passions. But greed and ambition in the rich, and in the poor the hatred of labour and the love of present ease and enjoyment, are the passions that drive men to invade property, passions far steadier in their working and far more universal in their influence. Wherever there is great property, there is great inequality. For every very rich man there must be at least five hundred poor ones, and the wealth of the few presupposes the poverty of the many. The wealth of the rich rouses the resentment of the poor, who are often both driven by want and spurred by envy to invade his possessions. It is only under the shelter of the civil magistrate that the owner of valuable property, gained by the labour of many years or perhaps of many successive generations, can sleep a single night in security. He is at all times surrounded by unknown enemies whom he can never appease, though he never provoked them, and from whose injustice he can be protected only by the powerful arm of the civil magistrate, kept constantly raised to punish it. The acquisition of valuable and extensive property, then, necessarily requires the establishment of civil government. Where there is no property, or at least none worth more than two or three days' labour, civil government is not so necessary.

Civil government presupposes a certain subordination. But just as the need for civil government gradually grows up with the acquisition of valuable property, so the chief causes that naturally produce subordination gradually grow up with the growth of that valuable property.

The causes or circumstances that naturally produce subordination, that naturally, and prior to any civil institution, give some men some superiority over most of their fellows, seem to be four in number.

The first of these causes is the superiority of personal qualities, of bodily strength, beauty, and agility, and of wisdom and virtue, of prudence, justice, fortitude, and moderation of mind. The qualities of the body, unless backed by those of the mind, can give little authority in any period of society. He is a very strong man indeed who can force two weak ones to obey him by mere bodily strength. Only the qualities of the mind can give very great authority. But these are invisible qualities, always disputable and generally disputed. No society, barbarous or civilized, has ever found it convenient to settle the rules of precedence in rank and subordination according to those invisible qualities, but rather according to something plainer and more palpable.

The second of these causes is the superiority of age. An old man, provided his age is not so far advanced as to raise the suspicion of senility, is everywhere more respected than a young man of equal rank, fortune, and abilities. Among nations of hunters, such as the native tribes of North America, age is the sole basis of rank and precedence. Among them, father is the title of a superior, brother of an equal, and son of an inferior. In the most prosperous and civilized nations, age settles rank among those who are in every other respect equal, and among whom, therefore, there is nothing else to settle it. Among brothers and among sisters the eldest always takes precedence, and in the succession to the family estate, whatever cannot be divided but must go whole to one person, such as a title of honour, is in most cases given to the eldest. Age is a plain and palpable quality that admits of no dispute.

The third of these causes is the superiority of fortune. The authority of riches, though great in every age of society, is perhaps greatest in the crudest ages that admit of any considerable inequality of fortune. A Tartar chief whose growing flocks and herds are enough to support a thousand men can hardly use that increase in any way except to support a thousand men. The crude state of his society offers him no manufactured goods, no trinkets or baubles of any kind, for which he could exchange the surplus of his raw produce beyond his own consumption. The thousand men he thus supports, depending entirely on him for their subsistence, must both obey his orders in war and submit to his jurisdiction in peace. He is necessarily both their general and their judge, and his chieftainship is the inevitable result of his superior fortune. In a prosperous and civilized society, a man may have a much greater fortune and yet not be able to command a dozen people. Though the produce of his estate may be enough to support, and perhaps actually does support, more than a thousand people, yet since those people pay for everything they get from him, since he gives hardly anything to anyone except in exchange for an equivalent, there is scarcely anyone who considers himself wholly dependent on him, and his authority reaches only over a few household servants. Still, the authority of fortune is very great even in a prosperous and civilized society. That it is far greater than that of either age or personal qualities has been the constant complaint of every period of society that admitted of any considerable inequality of fortune. The first period of society, that of hunters, admits of no such inequality. Universal poverty establishes their universal equality, and the superiority of age or of personal qualities is the feeble but sole foundation of authority and subordination. There is therefore little or no authority or subordination in this period of society. The second period, that of shepherds, admits of very great inequalities of fortune, and there is no period in which superior fortune gives so great an authority to those who possess it. Accordingly, there is no period in which authority and subordination are more perfectly established. The authority of an Arab sharif is very great; that of a Tartar khan is altogether despotic.

The fourth of these causes is the superiority of birth. Superiority of birth presupposes an ancient superiority of fortune in the family of the person who claims it. All families are equally ancient, and the ancestors of the prince, though they may be better known, can hardly be more numerous than those of the beggar. Antiquity of family means everywhere the antiquity either of wealth, or of that greatness which is commonly either founded on wealth or accompanied by it. Upstart greatness is everywhere less respected than ancient greatness. The hatred of usurpers and the love of an ancient monarch's family are largely founded on the contempt men naturally feel for the former and the reverence they feel for the latter. Just as a military officer submits without reluctance to the authority of a superior who has always commanded him, but cannot bear to have his inferior set over his head, so men easily submit to a family to whom they and their ancestors have always submitted, but are fired with indignation when another family, in whom they had never acknowledged any such superiority, claims dominion over them.

The distinction of birth, coming after the inequality of fortune, can have no place among nations of hunters, where all men, being equal in fortune, must likewise be very nearly equal in birth. The son of a wise and brave man may indeed, even among them, be somewhat more respected than a man of equal merit who has the misfortune to be the son of a fool or a coward. But the difference will not be very great; and there never was, I believe, a great family in the world whose distinction came entirely from inherited wisdom and virtue.

The distinction of birth not only may but always does take place among nations of shepherds. Such nations are always strangers to every sort of luxury, and great wealth can hardly ever be squandered among them by reckless extravagance. There are accordingly no nations richer in families revered and honoured for their descent from a long line of great and illustrious ancestors, because there are no nations among whom wealth is likely to stay longer in the same families.

Birth and fortune are clearly the two circumstances that chiefly raise one man above another. They are the two great sources of personal distinction, and so the principal causes that naturally establish authority and subordination among men. Among nations of shepherds, both causes operate at full force. The great shepherd or herdsman, respected for his great wealth and the great number of those who depend on him for subsistence, and revered for the nobility of his birth and the immemorial antiquity of his illustrious family, has a natural authority over all the lesser shepherds or herdsmen of his horde or clan. He can command the united force of more people than any of them. His military power is greater than any of theirs. In war they are all naturally inclined to muster under his banner rather than under anyone else's, and his birth and fortune thus naturally bring him a sort of executive power. And by commanding the united force of more people than any of them, he is also best able to compel any one of them who has wronged another to make amends. He is therefore the man to whom all those too weak to defend themselves naturally look for protection. It is to him that they naturally complain of the wrongs they think have been done to them, and his intervention in such cases is more readily accepted, even by the person complained of, than anyone else's would be. His birth and fortune thus naturally bring him a sort of judicial authority.

It is in the age of shepherds, the second period of society, that inequality of fortune first arises and introduces among men a degree of authority and subordination that could not possibly have existed before. It thereby introduces some degree of the civil government that is indispensable to its own preservation, and it seems to do this naturally, even apart from any consideration of that necessity. The consideration of that necessity comes, no doubt, afterwards, and does much to maintain and secure that authority and subordination. The rich in particular have a necessary interest in supporting the order of things that alone can secure them in possession of their own advantages. Men of lesser wealth combine to defend those of greater wealth in possession of their property, so that men of greater wealth will combine to defend them in possession of theirs. All the lesser shepherds and herdsmen feel that the security of their own herds and flocks depends on the security of the great shepherd or herdsman's, that the maintenance of their lesser authority depends on his greater authority, and that their subordination to him is what gives him the power to keep their own inferiors in subordination to them. They form a sort of little nobility, who feel an interest in defending the property and supporting the authority of their own little sovereign, so that he may be able to defend their property and support their authority. Civil government, so far as it is set up for the security of property, is in reality set up for the defence of the rich against the poor, or of those who have some property against those who have none at all.

The judicial authority of such a sovereign, however, far from being a source of expense, was for a long time a source of revenue to him. The people who came to him for justice were always willing to pay for it, and a gift never failed to accompany a petition. And once the sovereign's authority was thoroughly established, the person found guilty was forced, on top of the compensation he had to make to the injured party, to pay a fine to the sovereign as well. He had caused trouble, he had disturbed and broken the peace of his lord the king, and for those offences a fine was thought due. In the Tartar governments of Asia, and in the governments of Europe founded by the German and Scythian nations who overturned the Roman empire, the administration of justice was a considerable source of revenue both to the sovereign and to all the lesser chiefs or lords who exercised any particular jurisdiction under him, whether over some particular tribe or clan or over some particular territory or district. Originally both the sovereign and the inferior chiefs used to exercise this jurisdiction in person. Afterwards they universally found it convenient to delegate it to some deputy, bailiff, or judge. This deputy, however, was still obliged to account to his principal for the profits of the jurisdiction. Whoever reads the instructions given to the circuit judges in the time of Henry II (they are to be found in Tyrrell's History of England) will see clearly that those judges were a sort of travelling agents, sent round the country to collect certain branches of the king's revenue. In those days the administration of justice not only brought the sovereign a certain revenue, but raising that revenue seems to have been one of the principal advantages he hoped to gain from administering justice.

This scheme of making the administration of justice serve the purposes of revenue could hardly fail to produce several very gross abuses. The person who applied for justice with a large gift in his hand was likely to get rather more than justice, while the one who applied with a small gift was likely to get rather less. Justice, too, might often be delayed so that the gift might be repeated. And the fine on the person complained of might often suggest a very strong reason for finding him in the wrong, even when he really was not. That such abuses were far from uncommon, the ancient history of every country in Europe bears witness.

When the sovereign or chief exercises his judicial authority in person, however much he may abuse it, it must have been almost impossible to get any redress, because there could seldom be anyone powerful enough to call him to account. When he exercised it through a bailiff, redress might sometimes be had. If the bailiff had committed an act of injustice for his own benefit only, the sovereign himself might not always be unwilling to punish him or make him repair the wrong. But if it was for the sovereign's benefit, if he had committed some act of oppression in order to curry favour with the man who had appointed him and might promote him, redress would, in most cases, be as impossible as if the sovereign had committed it himself. Accordingly, in all barbarous governments, and in those ancient governments of Europe in particular that were founded on the ruins of the Roman empire, the administration of justice appears to have been for a long time extremely corrupt, far from equal and impartial even under the best monarchs, and altogether profligate under the worst.

Among nations of shepherds, where the sovereign or chief is only the greatest shepherd or herdsman of the horde or clan, he is supported in the same way as any of his vassals or subjects, by the increase of his own herds or flocks. Among those nations of farmers who have only just emerged from the shepherd state and are not much advanced beyond it, such as the Greek tribes appear to have been about the time of the Trojan war, and our German and Scythian ancestors when they first settled on the ruins of the western empire, the sovereign or chief is likewise only the greatest landlord of the country, and is supported in the same way as any other landlord, by a revenue drawn from his own private estate, or from what in modern Europe was called the demesne of the crown. His subjects, on ordinary occasions, contribute nothing to his support, except when they need his authority to protect them from the oppression of some of their fellow subjects. The gifts they make him on such occasions make up the whole ordinary revenue, the whole of the emoluments that, except perhaps on some very extraordinary emergency, he derives from his dominion over them. When Agamemnon, in Homer, offers Achilles the sovereignty of seven Greek cities in return for his friendship, the sole advantage he names as likely to come of it is that the people would honour him with gifts. As long as such gifts, as long as the emoluments of justice, or what may be called the fees of court, made up in this way the whole ordinary revenue the sovereign drew from his sovereignty, he could hardly be expected, nor could it even decently be proposed, to give them up altogether. It might be proposed, and frequently was, that he should regulate and fix them. But once they had been so regulated and fixed, how to stop an all-powerful person from extending them beyond those regulations was still very difficult, not to say impossible. So while this state of things lasted, the corruption of justice, which naturally followed from the arbitrary and uncertain nature of those gifts, scarcely admitted of any effective remedy.

Eventually, though, several pressures changed this. The chief one was the steadily rising cost of defending a nation against foreign invasion, which left the sovereign's private estate far too small to cover the expenses of running the state. Once the people had to chip in for their own security through taxes of various kinds, it became a common rule that no gift could be accepted, on any pretext, for the administration of justice, whether by the sovereign or by his bailiffs and deputies, the judges. The thinking seems to have been that such gifts were easier to abolish outright than to regulate and pin down. Judges were given fixed salaries, meant to make up for the share of the old fees that they would now lose, just as the new taxes more than made up for the sovereign's lost share. Justice was now described as being administered free of charge.

In reality, though, justice was never administered free of charge in any country. Lawyers and attorneys, at the very least, always have to be paid by the parties; if they weren't, they would do their job even worse than they already do. The fees paid each year to lawyers and attorneys add up, in every court, to far more than the judges' salaries. Having the salaries paid by the crown does little anywhere to reduce the unavoidable cost of a lawsuit. But the point of barring judges from taking any gift or fee from the parties was not so much to cut the cost as to prevent the corruption of justice.

The office of judge is so honourable in itself that men are willing to take it on even when the pay is very small. The lesser office of justice of the peace involves a good deal of trouble and, in most cases, no pay at all, yet most of our country gentlemen aspire to it. The salaries of all the various judges, high and low, together with the whole cost of administering and carrying out justice, even where it is not run very economically, make up only a tiny share of total government spending in any civilized country.

The whole cost of justice could easily be covered by court fees as well, and the public revenue could thereby be relieved of a definite, if modest, burden without putting the administration of justice at any real risk of corruption. Court fees are hard to regulate effectively when someone as powerful as the sovereign shares in them and draws a sizeable part of his revenue from them. They are easy to regulate when the judge is the main person who can profit from them. The law can readily compel a judge to respect the regulation, even though it might not always be able to make the sovereign respect it. Suppose the fees are precisely fixed and known, and are paid all at once, at a set point in every case, into the hands of a cashier or receiver, who then distributes them in known proportions among the various judges after the case is decided, and only then. In that arrangement there seems to be no more danger of corruption than if such fees were banned altogether. Without adding much to the cost of a lawsuit, these fees could be made fully sufficient to cover the whole expense of justice. And since the judges would not be paid until the case was settled, the fees might also spur the court to be diligent in examining and deciding it. In courts made up of a large number of judges, if each judge's share were set in proportion to the hours and days he had spent examining the case, whether in court or in a committee by the court's order, the fees might encourage the diligence of each individual judge. Public services are never better performed than when the reward comes only as a result of performing them, and is proportioned to the effort put in. In the various parliaments of France, the court fees (called épices and vacations) make up by far the greater part of the judges' earnings. After all deductions, the net salary the crown pays a counsellor or judge in the parliament of Toulouse, the second parliament of the kingdom in rank and dignity, comes to only 150 livres, about £6 11s. sterling a year. Seven years or so ago, that sum was the usual yearly wage of an ordinary footman in that same place. These épices, too, are distributed according to the judges' diligence. A diligent judge earns a comfortable, if moderate, income from his office; an idle one gets little beyond his salary. In many ways these parliaments may not be very convenient courts of justice, but they have never been accused, and seem never even to have been suspected, of corruption.

Court fees seem originally to have been the chief support of England's various courts of justice. Each court tried to attract as much business as it could, and for that reason was willing to take on many suits that were never meant to fall within its jurisdiction. The court of King's Bench, set up to try criminal cases only, took on civil suits, with the plaintiff claiming that the defendant, in failing to do him justice, had committed some trespass or misdemeanour. The court of Exchequer, set up to collect the king's revenue and to enforce payment only of debts owed to the king, took on all other contract debts, with the plaintiff alleging that he could not pay the king because the defendant would not pay him. Thanks to such fictions, it often came down entirely to the parties which court they chose to have their case tried in, and each court tried, by faster and fairer service, to draw as many cases to itself as it could. England's present admirable system of courts was perhaps shaped, in large part, by this rivalry that once existed among their respective judges, each judge striving to provide, in his own court, the quickest and most effective remedy the law would allow for every kind of injustice. Originally, the courts of law awarded damages only for breach of contract. The court of Chancery, as a court of conscience, was the first to take it upon itself to enforce the specific performance of agreements. When a breach of contract amounted to the non-payment of money, the loss could be made good only by ordering payment, which was equivalent to specific performance of the agreement; in such cases, then, the remedy offered by the courts of law was enough. It was not enough in other cases. When a tenant sued his lord for having unjustly turned him out of his lease, the damages he recovered were nothing like equivalent to possessing the land. For a time, therefore, such cases all went to the court of Chancery, to the considerable loss of the courts of law. It was to win such cases back for themselves that the courts of law are said to have invented the artificial and fictitious writ of ejectment, the most effective remedy for an unjust eviction or dispossession of land.

A stamp duty on the legal proceedings of each particular court, collected by that court and used to maintain its judges and other officers, could in the same way provide enough revenue to cover the cost of administering justice without putting any burden on society's general revenue. In this case, though, the judges might be tempted to needlessly multiply the proceedings in every case, so as to boost the yield of the stamp duty as much as possible. In modern Europe it has been the custom, on most occasions, to set the pay of attorneys and court clerks according to the number of pages they had to write, while the court required each page to hold a certain number of lines and each line a certain number of words. To increase their pay, attorneys and clerks have found ways to pad out the wording far beyond any need, corrupting the legal language of, I believe, every court of justice in Europe. A similar temptation might likewise corrupt the form of legal proceedings.

But whether the administration of justice is arranged to cover its own costs, or the judges are supported by fixed salaries paid from some other fund, it does not seem necessary that the person or persons holding executive power should be put in charge of that fund or of paying those salaries. The fund might come from the rent of landed estates, with each estate's management entrusted to the particular court it was meant to support. It might even come from the interest on a sum of money, the lending out of which could likewise be entrusted to the court it was meant to support. A part of the salary of the judges of the Court of Session in Scotland, though only a small part, does come from the interest on a sum of money. Yet the inevitable instability of such a fund seems to make it unsuitable for maintaining an institution that ought to last forever.

The separation of judicial power from executive power seems originally to have arisen from the growing business of society as it became more advanced. Administering justice grew so laborious and so complicated a duty that it demanded the undivided attention of whoever was charged with it. Since the person holding executive power had no time to attend to private cases himself, a deputy was appointed to decide them in his place. As Rome rose to greatness, the consul became too taken up with the state's political affairs to attend to the administration of justice, so a praetor was appointed to administer it in his stead. As the European monarchies that were built on the ruins of the Roman empire developed, the sovereigns and great lords came everywhere to regard administering justice as an office both too laborious and too lowly to carry out in person. So they all rid themselves of it by appointing a deputy, a bailiff or judge.

When judicial power is joined to executive power, it is scarcely possible that justice will not often be sacrificed to what is commonly called politics. Those entrusted with the great interests of the state may, even without any corrupt aim, sometimes think it necessary to sacrifice a private individual's rights to those interests. Yet every individual's liberty, and his sense of his own security, depends on justice being administered impartially. To make every individual feel perfectly secure in possessing every right that belongs to him, it is not enough that the judicial power be separated from the executive; it must also be made as independent of that power as possible. A judge should not be liable to be removed from office at the whim of that power. The regular payment of his salary should not depend on the goodwill, or even on the thrift, of that power.
Part III. The Expense of Public Works and Public Institutions.

The third and final duty of the sovereign or commonwealth is to set up and maintain those public institutions and public works which, though they may be of the very highest benefit to a great society, are nonetheless of such a kind that the profit could never repay the cost to any individual or small group of individuals. For that reason, no individual or small group can be expected to build or maintain them. Carrying out this duty also requires very different levels of expense at different stages of society.

Apart from the public institutions and public works needed for the defence of society and for the administration of justice, both already discussed, the other works and institutions of this kind are chiefly meant either to make society's commerce easier or to promote the instruction of the people. Institutions for instruction are of two sorts: those for educating the young, and those for instructing people of all ages. Considering how the cost of these different sorts of public works and institutions can best be met will divide this third part of the present chapter into three separate articles.
Article I. The Public Works and Institutions for Facilitating the Commerce of Society.
First, those needed for facilitating commerce in general.

It needs no proof that building and maintaining the public works that ease a country's commerce, such as good roads, bridges, navigable canals, harbours, and so on, must require very different levels of expense at different stages of society. The cost of making and maintaining a country's public roads must clearly rise along with the annual produce of its land and labour, that is, with the quantity and weight of the goods that have to be carried along those roads. A bridge's strength must match the number and weight of the vehicles likely to cross it. The depth and water supply of a navigable canal must match the number and tonnage of the barges likely to carry goods on it, and a harbour's size must match the number of ships likely to take shelter in it.

It does not seem necessary that the cost of these public works be met from what is commonly called the public revenue, whose collection and use are in most countries assigned to the executive power. Most such public works can easily be managed so as to yield a revenue of their own, enough to cover their own cost without putting any burden on society's general revenue.

A highway, a bridge, or a navigable canal, for instance, can in most cases be both built and maintained by a small toll on the vehicles that use them, and a harbour by a moderate port duty on the tonnage of the ships that load or unload in it. The coinage, another institution for facilitating commerce, in many countries not only covers its own cost but yields the sovereign a small revenue, a seigniorage. The post office, another institution serving the same purpose, in almost every country yields the sovereign a very considerable revenue over and above covering its own cost.

When the vehicles that pass over a highway or bridge, and the barges that sail on a navigable canal, pay a toll in proportion to their weight or tonnage, they pay for the upkeep of those works exactly in proportion to the wear and tear they cause. It seems scarcely possible to devise a fairer way of maintaining such works. This tax or toll, though advanced by the carrier, is ultimately paid by the consumer, who always has it charged to him in the price of the goods. But since such works greatly reduce the cost of carriage, the goods reach the consumer cheaper despite the toll than they otherwise would have, because the toll raises their price less than the cheaper carriage lowers it. So the person who finally pays this tax gains more from the works than he loses by the payment, and his payment is exactly proportioned to his gain. It is really no more than a part of that gain which he has to give up in order to keep the rest. It seems impossible to imagine a fairer method of raising a tax. When the toll on luxury vehicles, such as coaches and post-chaises, is set somewhat higher in proportion to their weight than the toll on vehicles of necessary use, such as carts and wagons, the indolence and vanity of the rich are made, in a very easy way, to relieve the poor by lowering the cost of transporting heavy goods to all parts of the country.

When highways, bridges, canals, and the like are built and supported in this way by the commerce carried on through them, they can be built only where that commerce calls for them, and so only where it is right to build them. Their cost, too, and their grandeur and magnificence, must be matched to what that commerce can afford to pay. A magnificent highway cannot be run through a barren region with little or no commerce, or merely because it happens to lead to the country villa of the provincial intendant, or to that of some great lord whom the intendant finds it convenient to court. A great bridge cannot be thrown over a river at a spot where nobody crosses, or merely to embellish the view from the windows of a nearby palace, things that sometimes happen in countries where works of this kind are paid for out of some revenue other than what they can generate themselves.

In several parts of Europe, the toll or lock duty on a canal belongs to private persons, whose own interest forces them to keep the canal up. If it is not kept in reasonable order, navigation stops altogether, and with it all the profit they can make from the tolls. If those tolls were placed under the management of commissioners with no stake in them, they might be less attentive to maintaining the works that produced them. The Canal of Languedoc cost the king of France and the province upwards of thirteen million livres, which, at twenty-eight livres to the mark of silver, the value of French money at the end of the last century, came to upwards of nine hundred thousand pounds sterling. When that great work was finished, the surest way found of keeping it in constant repair was to make a present of the tolls to Riquet, the engineer who designed and directed it. Those tolls now form a very large estate for the various branches of that gentleman's family, who therefore have a strong interest in keeping the work in constant repair. Had the tolls been placed under commissioners with no such interest, they might perhaps have been frittered away on ornamental and needless expenses while the most essential parts of the works were left to fall into ruin.

The tolls for maintaining a highway cannot safely be made the property of private persons. A highway, even if entirely neglected, does not become wholly impassable, whereas a canal does. The owners of the tolls on a highway might therefore neglect its repair altogether and yet keep levying nearly the same tolls. It is fitting, then, that the tolls for maintaining such a work be placed under the management of commissioners or trustees.

In Great Britain the abuses that trustees have committed in managing these tolls have, in many cases, been very justly complained of. At many turnpikes, it is said, the money collected is more than twice what is needed to do the work in the most complete way, work which is often done very shoddily and sometimes not done at all. It must be noted that this system of repairing highways by such tolls is not of very long standing, so we should not be surprised if it has not yet reached the level of perfection it seems capable of. If unsuitable and improper persons are often appointed as trustees, and if proper courts of inspection and audit have not yet been set up to oversee their conduct and to bring the tolls down to no more than is barely enough to do the work, the newness of the institution both explains and excuses these defects, most of which may, through the wisdom of parliament, be gradually put right in due course.

The money collected at the various turnpikes in Great Britain is supposed to exceed so far what is needed to repair the roads that the savings which, with proper economy, might be made from it have been regarded, even by some ministers, as a great resource that might at some point be applied to the needs of the state. It has been argued that if the government took the turnpikes into its own hands and used soldiers, who would work for a very small addition to their pay, it could keep the roads in good order at far less cost than trustees can, who have no workmen to employ but men who depend entirely on their wages for a living. A great revenue, perhaps half a million, it has been claimed, might be gained in this way without laying any new burden on the people, and the turnpike roads might be made to contribute to the general expense of the state, just as the post office does at present. (Since publishing the first two editions of this book, I have good reason to believe that all the turnpike tolls collected in Great Britain do not yield a net revenue amounting to half a million, a sum which, under government management, would not be enough to keep five of the kingdom's principal roads in repair.)

I have no doubt that a considerable revenue might be gained in this way, though probably nothing like as much as the promoters of this plan have supposed. The plan itself, however, seems open to several very serious objections.

First, if the tolls collected at the turnpikes were ever treated as one of the resources for meeting the needs of the state, they would certainly be raised as those needs were thought to require. Given Britain's policy, then, they would probably be raised very fast. The ease with which a great revenue could be drawn from them would probably tempt the administration to turn to this resource very often. Although it may be more than doubtful whether half a million could by any economy be saved out of the present tolls, it can scarcely be doubted that a million might be saved if they were doubled, and perhaps two million if they were tripled. (I now have good reason to believe these conjectural sums are far too large.) This great revenue, too, could be collected without appointing a single new officer to gather it in. But if the turnpike tolls were continually raised in this way, then instead of easing the country's inland commerce as they now do, they would soon become a very great burden on it. The cost of carrying all heavy goods from one part of the country to another would soon rise so much, and the market for all such goods would consequently be so narrowed, that their production would be largely discouraged, and the most important branches of the country's domestic industry would be wiped out altogether.

Second, a tax on vehicles in proportion to their weight, though a very fair tax when used solely to repair the roads, is a very unfair one when used for any other purpose, or to meet the ordinary needs of the state. When used solely for repairing roads, each vehicle is supposed to pay exactly for the wear and tear it causes them. But when used for any other purpose, each vehicle is supposed to pay for more than that wear and tear, contributing as well to meeting some other need of the state. And since the turnpike toll raises the price of goods in proportion to their weight rather than their value, it falls chiefly on consumers of coarse and bulky goods, not on those of precious and light ones. So whatever need of the state this tax might be meant to meet, it would be met chiefly at the expense of the poor, not the rich, at the expense of those least able to bear it, not those most able.

Third, if the government were ever to neglect the repair of the highways, it would be even harder than it is now to compel any part of the turnpike tolls to be applied properly. A large revenue might thus be collected from the people without any of it being applied to the only purpose to which a revenue raised in this way ought ever to be applied. If the meanness and poverty of the trustees of turnpike roads sometimes make it hard, even now, to oblige them to repair their roads, their wealth and greatness would make it ten times harder in the case here supposed.

In France the funds set aside for repairing the highways are under the direct control of the executive power. Those funds consist partly of a certain number of days' labour that the country people, in most parts of Europe, are obliged to give to repairing the roads, and partly of whatever portion of the state's general revenue the king chooses to spare from his other expenses.

By the ancient law of France, as well as that of most other parts of Europe, the labour of the country people was directed by a local or provincial magistracy that did not depend directly on the king's council.
