But under the present practice, both the labour of the country people and whatever other fund the king may assign to repairing the highways in any particular province or généralité are entirely under the management of the intendant, an officer who is appointed and removed by the king's council, takes his orders from it, and is in constant correspondence with it. As despotism advances, the authority of the executive power gradually absorbs that of every other power in the state and takes to itself the management of every branch of revenue meant for any public purpose. In France, however, the great post roads, the roads connecting the kingdom's principal towns, are generally kept in good order, and in some provinces are even far superior to most of England's turnpike roads. But what we call the cross roads, that is, by far the greater part of the country's roads, are entirely neglected, and in many places are absolutely impassable for any heavy vehicle. In some places it is even dangerous to travel on horseback, and mules are the only conveyance that can be safely trusted. The proud minister of an ostentatious court may often take pleasure in carrying out a work of splendour and magnificence, such as a great highway, which is frequently seen by the leading nobility, whose applause not only flatters his vanity but even helps to support his interest at court. But to carry out a great many small works, in which nothing that can be done makes any great show or stirs the least admiration in any traveller, and which in short have nothing to recommend them but their extreme usefulness, is a business that seems in every way too mean and paltry to deserve the attention of so great a magistrate. Under such an administration, then, such works are almost always entirely neglected.

In China and several other governments of Asia, the executive power takes charge both of repairing the highways and of maintaining the navigable canals. In the instructions given to the governor of each province, these matters are said to be constantly urged on him, and the court's judgment of his conduct is largely governed by the attention he appears to have paid to this part of his instructions. This branch of public administration is accordingly said to be much attended to in all those countries, but especially in China, where the highways and, still more, the navigable canals are claimed to far surpass anything of the same kind known in Europe. Yet the accounts of these works that have reached Europe have generally been drawn up by gullible and wondering travellers, often by stupid and lying missionaries. Had they been examined by more intelligent eyes, and reported by more faithful witnesses, they would perhaps not seem so wonderful. The account Bernier gives of some works of this kind in Hindustan falls well short of what other travellers, more given to the marvellous than he was, had reported of them. It may also be, in those countries as in France, that the great roads and great links likely to be talked of at court and in the capital are attended to, and all the rest neglected. Besides, in China, Hindustan, and several other governments of Asia, the sovereign's revenue comes almost entirely from a land tax or land rent that rises and falls with the rise and fall of the land's annual produce. The sovereign's great interest, his revenue, is therefore necessarily and directly bound up in those countries with the cultivation of the land, with the size of its produce, and with the value of that produce. But to make that produce as great and as valuable as possible, it has to be given as wide a market as possible, and this means setting up the freest, easiest, and least costly communication between all parts of the country, which can be done only by the best roads and the best navigable canals. In no part of Europe, however, does the sovereign's revenue come chiefly from a land tax or land rent. In all the great kingdoms of Europe, perhaps, the greater part of it may ultimately depend on the produce of the land, but that dependence is neither so direct nor so obvious. In Europe, therefore, the sovereign does not feel himself so directly called upon to promote the increase, in both quantity and value, of the land's produce, or to provide the widest possible market for it by maintaining good roads and canals. So even if it were true, which I rather doubt, that in some parts of Asia this department of public administration is very properly managed by the executive power, there is not the slightest likelihood that, as things now stand, it could be tolerably managed by that power in any part of Europe.

Even those public works that are of such a kind that they cannot yield any revenue to maintain themselves, but whose usefulness is more or less confined to one particular place or district, are always better maintained by a local or provincial revenue under the management of a local and provincial administration than by the general revenue of the state, which the executive power must always control. If the streets of London were lit and paved at the Treasury's expense, is there any likelihood they would be as well lit and paved as they are now, or even done as cheaply? The cost, besides, instead of being raised by a local tax on the inhabitants of each particular street, parish, or district in London, would in that case be met out of the state's general revenue, and so be raised by a tax on all the inhabitants of the kingdom, most of whom get no benefit at all from the lighting and paving of London's streets.

The abuses that sometimes creep into the local and provincial administration of a local and provincial revenue, however enormous they may appear, are in reality almost always trifling compared with those that commonly occur in administering and spending the revenue of a great empire. They are, besides, much more easily corrected. Under the local or provincial administration of the justices of the peace in Great Britain, the six days' labour that the country people are obliged to give to repairing the highways is not always, perhaps, very wisely used, but it is hardly ever exacted with any cruelty or oppression. In France, under the administration of the intendants, the labour is not always more wisely used, and it is frequently exacted in the most cruel and oppressive way. These corvées, as they are called, are one of the chief instruments of tyranny by which those officers punish any parish or commune unlucky enough to fall under their displeasure.
The Public Works and Institutions Needed for Facilitating Particular Branches of Commerce.

The aim of the public works and institutions mentioned above is to facilitate commerce in general. But to facilitate certain particular branches of it, particular institutions are needed, which in turn require a particular and extraordinary expense.

Some particular branches of commerce carried on with barbarous and uncivilized nations require extraordinary protection. An ordinary store or counting house could give little security to the goods of merchants trading to the western coast of Africa. To protect them from the barbarous natives, the place where the goods are kept has to be fortified to some degree. The disorders in the government of Hindustan have been thought to make a similar precaution necessary even among that mild and gentle people, and it was under pretence of securing their persons and property from violence that both the English and French East India companies were allowed to build the first forts they held in that country. Among other nations, whose vigorous government will allow no strangers to hold any fortified place within their territory, it may be necessary to keep some ambassador, minister, or consul, who can both settle, according to their own customs, the disputes arising among his own countrymen, and, in their disputes with the natives, use his public character to intervene with more authority and give them more powerful protection than they could expect from any private man. The interests of commerce have often made it necessary to keep ministers in foreign countries where the purposes of war or alliance would have required none. The trade of the Turkey Company first brought about the establishment of a permanent ambassador at Constantinople. The first English embassies to Russia arose entirely from commercial interests. The constant clashing of such interests, inevitable between the subjects of the different states of Europe, has probably given rise to the custom of keeping resident ambassadors or ministers in all neighbouring countries even in peacetime. This custom, unknown in ancient times, seems no older than the end of the fifteenth or the beginning of the sixteenth century, that is, the time when commerce first began to spread to most of the nations of Europe, and when they first began to attend to its interests.

It seems not unreasonable that the extraordinary expense which protecting any particular branch of commerce may cause should be met by a moderate tax on that particular branch, for example by a moderate fee paid by traders when they first enter it, or, more fairly, by a particular duty of so much per cent on the goods they import into, or export out of, the particular countries with which the trade is carried on. The protection of trade in general from pirates and freebooters is said to have given rise to the first establishment of customs duties. But if it was thought reasonable to lay a general tax on trade in order to cover the cost of protecting trade in general, it should seem equally reasonable to lay a particular tax on a particular branch of trade in order to cover the extraordinary cost of protecting that branch.

The protection of trade in general has always been regarded as essential to the defence of the commonwealth, and on that account a necessary part of the duty of the executive power. The collection and use of the general customs duties have therefore always been left to that power. But protecting any particular branch of trade is part of the general protection of trade, and so part of the duty of that power; and if nations always acted consistently, the particular duties levied for such particular protection should always have been left equally to its disposal. But in this, as in many other respects, nations have not always acted consistently, and in most of the commercial states of Europe particular companies of merchants have had the cunning to persuade the legislature to entrust to them the carrying out of this part of the sovereign's duty, together with all the powers necessarily connected with it.

These companies, though they may perhaps have been useful in first introducing some branches of commerce, by making at their own expense an experiment that the state might not think it prudent to make, have in the long run universally proved either burdensome or useless, and have either mismanaged or restricted the trade.

When such companies do not trade on a joint stock, but are obliged to admit any properly qualified person on payment of a certain fee and on his agreeing to submit to the company's regulations, each member trading on his own stock and at his own risk, they are called regulated companies. When they trade on a joint stock, each member sharing in the common profit or loss in proportion to his share in the stock, they are called joint-stock companies. Such companies, whether regulated or joint-stock, sometimes have exclusive privileges and sometimes do not.

Regulated companies resemble in every respect the trade guilds so common in the cities and towns of every country of Europe, and are a sort of enlarged monopoly of the same kind. Just as no inhabitant of a town can practise an incorporated trade without first obtaining his freedom in the guild, so in most cases no subject of the state can lawfully carry on any branch of foreign trade for which a regulated company exists without first becoming a member of that company. The monopoly is stricter or looser according to how difficult the terms of admission are, and according to how much authority the company's directors have, or how far it is in their power to arrange things so as to keep most of the trade to themselves and their particular friends. In the most ancient regulated companies, the privileges of apprenticeship were the same as in other guilds, and entitled a man who had served his time under a member of the company to become a member himself, either without paying any fee or on paying a much smaller one than was demanded of other people. The usual guild spirit, wherever the law does not restrain it, prevails in all regulated companies. When they have been allowed to act according to their natural bent, they have always, in order to confine the competition to as few people as possible, tried to subject the trade to many burdensome regulations. When the law has stopped them from doing this, they have become altogether useless and insignificant.

The regulated companies for foreign commerce that exist at present in Great Britain are the ancient Merchant Adventurers Company, now commonly called the Hamburgh Company, the Russia Company, the Eastland Company, the Turkey Company, and the African Company.

The terms of admission into the Hamburgh Company are now said to be quite easy, and the directors either have no power to subject the trade to any troublesome restraints or regulations, or at least have not lately used that power. It was not always so. About the middle of the last century the fine for admission was fifty pounds, and at one time a hundred, and the company's conduct was said to be extremely oppressive. In 1643, 1645, and 1661, the clothiers and free traders of the west of England complained of them to parliament as monopolists who restricted the trade and oppressed the country's manufactures. Although these complaints produced no act of parliament, they had probably so intimidated the company as to force it to reform its conduct; at least there have been no complaints against it since that time. By the 10th and 11th of William III, c. 6, the fine for admission into the Russia Company was reduced to five pounds, and by the 25th of Charles II, c. 7, that for admission into the Eastland Company to forty shillings, while at the same time Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, all the countries on the north side of the Baltic, were exempted from its exclusive charter. The conduct of these companies had probably given occasion to these two acts of parliament. Before that time Sir Josiah Child had described both these and the Hamburgh Company as extremely oppressive, and blamed their bad management for the low state of the trade we then carried on to the countries within their respective charters. But though such companies may not be very oppressive in the present day, they are certainly altogether useless. To be merely useless is perhaps the highest praise that can ever justly be given to a regulated company, and all three companies named above seem, in their present state, to deserve this praise.

The fine for admission into the Turkey Company was formerly twenty-five pounds for anyone under twenty-six, and fifty pounds for anyone older. Nobody but actual merchants could be admitted, a restriction that excluded all shopkeepers and retailers. By a by-law, no British manufactures could be exported to Turkey except in the company's general ships, and since those ships always sailed from the port of London, this restriction confined the trade to that expensive port, and the traders to those living in London and its neighbourhood. By another by-law, no one living within twenty miles of London, and not free of the city, could be admitted a member, a further restriction which, added to the first, necessarily excluded all but the freemen of London. Since the timing of the loading and sailing of those general ships depended entirely on the directors, they could easily fill them with their own goods and those of their particular friends, to the exclusion of others, who, they might claim, had made their proposals too late. In this state of things, then, the company was in every respect a strict and oppressive monopoly. These abuses gave rise to the act of the 26th of George II, c. 18, which reduced the fine for admission to twenty pounds for everyone, without distinction of age, and without any restriction to actual merchants or to the freemen of London; and which granted all such persons the liberty of exporting, from any port of Great Britain to any port in Turkey, all British goods whose export was not prohibited, on paying both the general customs duties and the particular duties assessed to cover the company's necessary expenses, and on submitting at the same time to the lawful authority of the British ambassador and consuls resident in Turkey and to the company's duly enacted by-laws. To prevent any oppression through those by-laws, the same act provided that if any seven members of the company felt aggrieved by any by-law enacted after the passing of this act, they might appeal to the Board of Trade and Plantations (whose authority has now passed to a committee of the Privy Council), provided the appeal was brought within twelve months after the by-law was enacted; and that if any seven members felt aggrieved by any by-law enacted before the passing of this act, they might bring a like appeal, provided it was within twelve months after the day on which this act was to take effect. Yet a single year's experience may not always be enough to show all the members of a great company the harmful tendency of a particular by-law; and if several of them discover it afterwards, neither the Board of Trade nor the committee of council can give them any redress. Besides, the aim of most of the by-laws of all regulated companies, as of all other guilds, is not so much to oppress those who are already members as to discourage others from becoming members, which can be done not only by a high fine but by many other contrivances. The constant aim of such companies is always to raise their own rate of profit as high as they can, and to keep the market, both for the goods they export and for those they import, as understocked as they can, which can be done only by restraining competition or discouraging new adventurers from entering the trade. A fine even of twenty pounds, moreover, though it may not be enough to discourage anyone from entering the Turkey trade intending to stay in it, may be enough to discourage a speculative merchant from risking a single venture in it. In every trade the regular established traders, even when not incorporated, naturally combine to raise profits, which can in no way be kept down to their proper level at all times so well as by the occasional competition of speculative adventurers. The Turkey trade, though to some extent opened up by this act of parliament, is still regarded by many people as very far from being altogether free. The Turkey Company helps to maintain an ambassador and two or three consuls who, like other public ministers, ought to be maintained entirely by the state, with the trade laid open to all His Majesty's subjects. The various taxes the company levies for this and other guild purposes might yield a revenue much more than enough to enable a state to maintain such ministers.

Sir Josiah Child observed that regulated companies, though they had often supported public ministers, had never maintained any forts or garrisons in the countries they traded with, whereas joint-stock companies frequently had. And indeed the former seem far less fit for this sort of service than the latter. First, the directors of a regulated company have no particular interest in the prosperity of the general trade of the company, for whose sake such forts and garrisons are maintained. The decline of that general trade may even often work to the advantage of their own private trade, since by reducing the number of their competitors it may let them both buy cheaper and sell dearer. The directors of a joint-stock company, by contrast, having only their share in the profits made on the common stock entrusted to their management, have no private trade of their own whose interest can be separated from that of the company's general trade. Their private interest is bound up with the prosperity of the company's general trade and with the upkeep of the forts and garrisons needed for its defence. They are therefore more likely to give the continual and careful attention that such upkeep necessarily requires. Second, the directors of a joint-stock company always have the management of a large capital, the company's joint stock, part of which they can often properly use in building, repairing, and maintaining such necessary forts and garrisons. But the directors of a regulated company, having the management of no common capital, have no other fund to use for this than the casual revenue from admission fees and from the guild duties imposed on the company's trade. So even if they had the same interest in maintaining such forts and garrisons, they can seldom have the same ability to make that attention effective. Maintaining a public minister, which requires scarcely any attention and only a moderate and limited expense, is a business much better suited both to the temper and to the abilities of a regulated company.

Long after Sir Josiah Child's time, however, in 1750, a regulated company was established, the present Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, which was expressly charged at first with maintaining all the British forts and garrisons lying between Cape Blanc and the Cape of Good Hope, and afterwards with maintaining only those lying between Cape Rouge and the Cape of Good Hope. The act establishing this company (the 23rd of George II, c. 31) seems to have had two distinct aims: first, to restrain effectively the oppressive and monopolizing spirit natural to the directors of a regulated company; and second, to force them, as far as possible, to give an attention, which is not natural to them, to maintaining forts and garrisons.

For the first of these aims, the fine for admission is limited to forty shillings. The company is forbidden to trade in its corporate capacity, or on a joint stock; to borrow money on its common seal; or to lay any restraints on the trade, which may be carried on freely from all places, and by all persons who are British subjects and have paid the fine. The government is in a committee of nine persons who meet in London but are chosen annually by the company's freemen at London, Bristol, and Liverpool, three from each place. No committee-man can stay in office for more than three years together. Any committee-man might be removed by the Board of Trade and Plantations, now by a committee of council, after being heard in his own defence. The committee are forbidden to export negroes from Africa or to import any African goods into Great Britain. But since they are charged with maintaining forts and garrisons, they may for that purpose export goods and stores of various kinds from Great Britain to Africa. Out of the money they receive from the company, they are allowed a sum, not exceeding eight hundred pounds, for the salaries of their clerks and agents at London, Bristol, and Liverpool, the rent of their offices at London, and all other expenses of management, commission, and agency in England. Whatever is left of this sum after meeting these various expenses, they may divide among themselves, as they think fit, as compensation for their trouble. Under this constitution it might have been expected that the spirit of monopoly would have been effectively restrained and the first of these aims sufficiently met. It seems, however, that it was not. Although by the 4th of George III, c. 20, the fort of Senegal with all its dependencies had been vested in the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, yet in the following year (by the 5th of George III, c. 44), not only Senegal and its dependencies, but the whole coast from the port of Sallee in South Barbary to Cape Rouge, was exempted from that company's jurisdiction, vested in the crown, and the trade to it declared free to all His Majesty's subjects. The company had been suspected of restraining the trade and of setting up some sort of improper monopoly. It is not, however, very easy to see how, under the regulations of the 23rd of George II, they could do so. In the printed debates of the House of Commons, not always the most reliable records of truth, I do nevertheless find that they have been accused of this. Since the nine members of the committee were all merchants, and the governors and factors in their various forts and settlements were all dependent on them, it is not unlikely that the latter gave special attention to the consignments and commissions of the former, which would set up a real monopoly.

For the second of these aims, maintaining the forts and garrisons, parliament has allotted them an annual sum, generally about £13,000. For the proper application of this sum the committee is obliged to account annually to the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, the account afterwards to be laid before parliament. But parliament, which gives so little attention to the application of millions, is not likely to give much to that of £13,000 a year; and the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, by profession and training, is not likely to be deeply versed in the proper expense of forts and garrisons. The captains of His Majesty's navy, indeed, or any other commissioned officers appointed by the Board of Admiralty, may inquire into the condition of the forts and garrisons and report their observations to that board. But that board seems to have no direct jurisdiction over the committee, nor any authority to correct those whose conduct it may thus inquire into; and the captains of His Majesty's navy, besides, are not supposed to be always deeply learned in the science of fortification. Removal from an office that can be held only for a term of three years, and whose lawful earnings, even during that term, are so very small, seems to be the utmost punishment any committee-man is liable to for any fault except outright malversation or embezzlement, whether of public money or of the company's; and the fear of such punishment can never weigh heavily enough to force continual and careful attention to a business he has no other interest in attending to. The committee are accused of having sent out bricks and stones from England to repair Cape Coast Castle on the coast of Guinea, a job for which parliament had several times granted an extraordinary sum of money. These bricks and stones, too, sent on so long a voyage, were said to be of such bad quality that the walls repaired with them had to be rebuilt from the foundation. The forts and garrisons lying north of Cape Rouge are not only maintained at the state's expense but are under the direct government of the executive power; and why those lying south of that cape, which too are maintained at least in part at the state's expense, should be under a different government, it does not seem easy even to imagine a good reason. The protection of the Mediterranean trade was the original purpose, or pretext, of the garrisons of Gibraltar and Minorca, and the maintenance and government of those garrisons have always, very properly, been committed not to the Turkey Company but to the executive power. The pride and dignity of that power consist largely in the extent of its dominion, and it is not very likely to fail in attention to what is needed for the defence of that dominion. The garrisons at Gibraltar and Minorca, accordingly, have never been neglected. Although Minorca has been taken twice, and is now probably lost forever, that disaster has never been blamed on any neglect by the executive power. I would not, however, be understood to hint that either of these expensive garrisons was ever, even in the smallest degree, necessary for the purpose for which they were originally torn from the Spanish monarchy. That dismemberment, perhaps, never served any real purpose except to alienate from England her natural ally, the king of Spain, and to unite the two principal branches of the house of Bourbon in a far closer and more lasting alliance than ties of blood could ever have produced.
Joint-stock companies, established either by royal charter or by act of parliament, differ in several respects not only from regulated companies but from private partnerships.

First, in a private partnership no partner can, without the consent of the company, transfer his share to another person or bring a new member into the company. Each member, however, may on proper notice withdraw from the partnership and demand from them payment of his share of the common stock. In a joint-stock company, by contrast, no member can demand payment of his share from the company, but each member can, without their consent, transfer his share to another person and thereby bring in a new member. The value of a share in a joint stock is always whatever price it will fetch in the market, and this may be greater or less, in any proportion, than the sum its owner stands credited for in the company's stock.

Second, in a private partnership each partner is liable for the debts the company contracts to the whole extent of his fortune. In a joint-stock company, by contrast, each partner is liable only to the extent of his share.

The trade of a joint-stock company is always managed by a court of directors. This court is, indeed, often subject in many respects to the control of a general court of proprietors. But most of these proprietors seldom pretend to understand anything of the company's business, and when no spirit of faction happens to prevail among them, they give themselves no trouble about it but contentedly receive whatever half-yearly or yearly dividend the directors think proper to make them. This total freedom from trouble and from risk beyond a fixed sum tempts many people to become adventurers in joint-stock companies who would on no account risk their fortunes in any private partnership. Such companies, therefore, commonly draw to themselves far greater stocks than any private partnership can boast of. The trading stock of the South Sea Company at one time amounted to upwards of thirty-three million eight hundred thousand pounds. The divided capital of the Bank of England at present amounts to ten million seven hundred and eighty thousand pounds. But since the directors of such companies manage other people's money rather than their own, it cannot well be expected that they will watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which the partners in a private partnership often watch over their own. Like the stewards of a rich man, they are apt to regard attention to small matters as beneath their master's dignity, and very easily excuse themselves from it. Negligence and extravagance, therefore, must always prevail, more or less, in the management of such a company's affairs. It is for this reason that joint-stock companies for foreign trade have seldom been able to hold their own in competition against private adventurers. Accordingly, they have very seldom succeeded without an exclusive privilege, and frequently have not succeeded even with one. Without an exclusive privilege they have commonly mismanaged the trade; with one they have both mismanaged and restricted it.

The Royal African Company, the predecessors of the present African Company, had an exclusive privilege by charter; but since that charter had not been confirmed by act of parliament, the trade, in consequence of the Declaration of Rights, was soon after the Revolution laid open to all His Majesty's subjects. The Hudson's Bay Company are, as to their legal rights, in the same position as the Royal African Company. Their exclusive charter has not been confirmed by act of parliament. The South Sea Company, as long as they continued to be a trading company, had an exclusive privilege confirmed by act of parliament, as likewise have the present United Company of Merchants Trading to the East Indies.

The Royal African Company soon found that they could not hold their own against private adventurers, whom, despite the Declaration of Rights, they continued for some time to call interlopers and to persecute as such. In 1698, however, the private adventurers were subjected to a duty of ten per cent on almost all the different branches of their trade, to be used by the company in maintaining their forts and garrisons. But despite this heavy tax the company were still unable to keep up the competition. Their stock and credit gradually declined. By 1712 their debts had grown so great that a particular act of parliament was thought necessary, both for their own security and for that of their creditors. It was enacted that the decision of two-thirds of these creditors, in number and value, should bind the rest, both as to the time to be allowed the company for paying their debts, and as to any other agreement that might be thought proper to make with them about those debts. By 1730 their affairs were in such disorder that they were altogether unable to maintain their forts and garrisons, the sole purpose and pretext of their institution. From that year until their final dissolution, parliament judged it necessary to allow the annual sum of £10,000 for that purpose. In 1732, after having been for many years losers by the trade of carrying negroes to the West Indies, they at last resolved to give it up altogether, to sell to the private traders to America the negroes they bought on the coast, and to employ their servants in a trade to the inland parts of Africa for gold dust, elephants' teeth, dyeing drugs, and so on. But their success in this more confined trade was no greater than in their former extensive one. Their affairs went on gradually declining until at last, being in every respect a bankrupt company, they were dissolved by act of parliament, and their forts and garrisons vested in the present regulated Company of Merchants Trading to Africa. Before the founding of the Royal African Company, three other joint-stock companies had been established in succession, one after another, for the African trade. They were all equally unsuccessful. Yet they all had exclusive charters which, though not confirmed by act of parliament, were in those days supposed to convey a real exclusive privilege.

The Hudson's Bay Company, before their misfortunes in the late war, had been far more fortunate than the Royal African Company. Their necessary expense is much smaller. The whole number of people they maintain in their various settlements and dwellings, which they have honoured with the name of forts, is said not to exceed a hundred and twenty persons. This number, however, is enough to prepare in advance the cargo of furs and other goods needed to load their ships, which, because of the ice, can seldom stay above six or eight weeks in those seas. Private adventurers could not, for several years, gain this advantage of having a cargo ready prepared, and without it there seems no possibility of trading to Hudson's Bay. The company's moderate capital, which is said not to exceed one hundred and ten thousand pounds, may besides be enough to enable them to engross the whole, or almost the whole, trade and surplus produce of the wretched though extensive country within their charter. No private adventurers, accordingly, have ever tried to trade to that country in competition with them. This company, therefore, have always enjoyed an exclusive trade in fact, though they may have no right to it in law. On top of all this, the company's moderate capital is said to be divided among a very small number of proprietors. But a joint-stock company made up of a small number of proprietors with a moderate capital comes very close to the nature of a private partnership, and may be capable of nearly the same degree of vigilance and attention. It is not to be wondered at, then, if, thanks to these various advantages, the Hudson's Bay Company had, before the late war, been able to carry on their trade with a considerable degree of success. It does not seem likely, however, that their profits ever came near to what the late Mr Dobbs imagined them. A much soberer and more judicious writer, Mr Anderson, author of the Historical and Chronological Deduction of Commerce, very justly observes that on examining the accounts Mr Dobbs himself has given, for several years together, of their exports and imports, and on making proper allowance for their extraordinary risk and expense, it does not appear that their profits deserve to be envied, or that they can much, if at all, exceed the ordinary profits of trade.

The South Sea Company never had any forts or garrisons to maintain, and so were entirely free of one great expense to which other joint-stock companies for foreign trade are subject; but they had an immense capital divided among an immense number of proprietors. It was naturally to be expected, then, that folly, negligence, and extravagance would prevail in the whole management of their affairs. The knavery and extravagance of their stock-jobbing schemes are well enough known, and explaining them would be beside the present subject. Their mercantile projects were not much better conducted. The first trade they engaged in was supplying the Spanish West Indies with negroes, of which (in consequence of what was called the Assiento Contract granted them by the Treaty of Utrecht) they had the exclusive privilege. But since little profit was expected from this trade, both the Portuguese and French companies that had held it on the same terms before them having been ruined by it, they were allowed, by way of compensation, to send annually a ship of a certain tonnage to trade directly to the Spanish West Indies. Of the ten voyages this annual ship was allowed to make, they are said to have gained considerably by one, that of the Royal Caroline in 1731, and to have been losers, more or less, by almost all the rest. Their factors and agents blamed their ill success on the extortion and oppression of the Spanish government, but it was perhaps chiefly owing to the extravagance and depredations of those very factors and agents, some of whom are said to have made great fortunes in a single year. In 1734 the company petitioned the king to be allowed to dispose of the trade and tonnage of their annual ship, because of the little profit they made by it, and to accept whatever equivalent they could get from the king of Spain.

In 1724 this company had taken up the whale fishery. Of this, indeed, they had no monopoly; but as long as they carried it on, no other British subjects appear to have engaged in it. Of the eight voyages their ships made to Greenland, they gained by one and lost by all the rest. After their eighth and last voyage, when they had sold their ships, stores, and equipment, they found that their whole loss on this branch, capital and interest included, came to upwards of £237,000.

In 1722 this company petitioned parliament to be allowed to divide their immense capital of more than thirty-three million eight hundred thousand pounds, the whole of which had been lent to government, into two equal parts: one half, or upwards of £16,900,000, to be placed on the same footing as other government annuities, and not liable for the debts contracted, or losses incurred, by the company's directors in pursuing their mercantile projects; the other half to remain as before, a trading stock, and liable for those debts and losses. The petition was too reasonable not to be granted. In 1733 they petitioned parliament again, that three-fourths of their trading stock might be turned into annuity stock, and only one-fourth left as trading stock, exposed to the hazards arising from their directors' bad management. Both their annuity and trading stocks had by this time been reduced by more than two million each, through various payments from government, so that this fourth came to only £3,662,784 8s. 6d. In 1748, all the company's claims on the king of Spain under the Assiento Contract were, by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, given up for what was supposed an equivalent. Their trade with the Spanish West Indies was ended; the remainder of their trading stock was turned into annuity stock; and the company ceased, in every respect, to be a trading company.

It ought to be noted that in the trade the South Sea Company carried on by means of their annual ship, the only trade by which they were ever expected to make any considerable profit, they were not without competitors, either in the foreign or in the home market. At Cartagena, Porto Bello, and La Vera Cruz they had to face the competition of the Spanish merchants, who brought from Cadiz to those markets European goods of the same kind as the outward cargo of their ship; and in England they had to face that of the English merchants, who imported from Cadiz goods of the Spanish West Indies of the same kind as the inward cargo. The goods of both the Spanish and English merchants were, indeed, perhaps subject to higher duties. But the loss caused by the negligence, extravagance, and malversation of the company's servants had probably been a far heavier tax than all those duties. That a joint-stock company should be able to carry on successfully any branch of foreign trade when private adventurers can come into any sort of open and fair competition with them seems contrary to all experience.

The old English East India Company was established in 1600 by a charter from Queen Elizabeth. In the first twelve voyages they fitted out for India they appear to have traded as a regulated company, with separate stocks, though only in the company's general ships. In 1612 they united into a joint stock. Their charter was exclusive, and, though not confirmed by act of parliament, was in those days supposed to convey a real exclusive privilege. For many years, therefore, they were not much troubled by interlopers. Their capital, which never exceeded £744,000, and of which £50 was a share, was not so excessive, nor their dealings so extensive, as to give either a pretext for gross negligence and extravagance or a cover for gross malversation. Despite some extraordinary losses, caused partly by the malice of the Dutch East India Company and partly by other accidents, they carried on a successful trade for many years. But in time, as the principles of liberty came to be better understood, it grew every day more and more doubtful how far a royal charter, not confirmed by act of parliament, could convey an exclusive privilege. On this question the decisions of the courts of justice were not uniform, but varied with the authority of government and the moods of the times. Interlopers multiplied against them, and towards the end of the reign of Charles II, throughout that of James II, and during part of that of William III, reduced them to great distress. In 1698 a proposal was made to parliament to advance two million to government at eight per cent, provided the subscribers were set up as a new East India company with exclusive privileges. The old East India Company offered seven hundred thousand pounds, nearly the whole of their capital, at four per cent on the same conditions. But such was the state of public credit at that time that it was more convenient for government to borrow two million at eight per cent than seven hundred thousand at four. The new subscribers' proposal was accepted, and a new East India company established as a result. The old company, however, had a right to continue their trade till 1701. They had, at the same time, very artfully subscribed three hundred and fifteen thousand pounds, in the name of their treasurer, into the stock of the new company. Through a careless wording of the act of parliament that vested the East India trade in the subscribers to this loan of two million, it did not clearly appear that they were all obliged to unite into a joint stock. A few private traders, whose subscriptions came to only seven thousand two hundred pounds, insisted on the privilege of trading separately on their own stocks and at their own risk. The old East India Company had a right to a separate trade on their own stock till 1701, and they also had, both before and after that date, a right, like that of other private traders, to a separate trade on the £315,000 they had subscribed into the stock of the new company. The competition of the two companies with the private traders, and with one another, is said to have very nearly ruined both. On a later occasion, in 1730, when a proposal was made to parliament to put the trade under the management of a regulated company, and thereby in some measure open it up, the East India Company, opposing this proposal, described in very strong terms what they thought had been the miserable effects of this competition at that time. In India, they said, it raised the price of goods so high that they were not worth buying; and in England, by overstocking the market, it sank their price so low that no profit could be made by them. That a more plentiful supply, to the great advantage and convenience of the public, must have greatly reduced the price of India goods in the English market cannot well be doubted; but that it should have greatly raised their price in the Indian market seems not very likely, since all the extra demand that competition could cause must have been but as a drop of water in the immense ocean of Indian commerce. Besides, an increase of demand, though it may sometimes raise the price of goods at first, never fails to lower it in the long run. It encourages production, and thereby increases the competition of the producers, who, in order to undersell one another, resort to new divisions of labour and new improvements of art that might otherwise never have been thought of. The miserable effects of which the company complained were cheaper consumption and the encouragement given to production, precisely the two effects which it is the great business of political economy to promote. The competition, however, of which they gave this doleful account had not been allowed to last long. In 1702 the two companies were in some measure united by a tripartite indenture, to which the queen was the third party; and in 1708 they were by act of parliament perfectly consolidated into one company, under their present name of the United Company of Merchants Trading to the East Indies. It was thought worth while to insert into this act a clause allowing the separate traders to continue their trade till Michaelmas 1711, but at the same time empowering the directors, on three years' notice, to buy out their little capital of seven thousand two hundred pounds, and thereby turn the whole stock of the company into a joint stock. By the same act, the company's capital, in consequence of a new loan to government, was raised from two million to three million two hundred thousand pounds. In 1743 the company advanced another million to government. But since this million was raised not by a call on the proprietors but by selling annuities and contracting bond debts, it did not increase the stock on which the proprietors could claim a dividend. It did, however, increase their trading stock, being equally liable with the other three million two hundred thousand pounds for the losses sustained, and debts contracted, by the company in pursuing their mercantile projects. From 1708, or at least from 1711, this company, freed from all competitors and fully established in the monopoly of the English trade to the East Indies, carried on a successful trade, and out of their profits made their proprietors a moderate dividend every year. During the French war that began in 1741, the ambition of Mr Dupleix, the French governor of Pondicherry, drew them into the wars of the Carnatic and into the politics of the Indian princes. After many signal successes and equally signal losses, they at last lost Madras, at that time their principal settlement in India. It was restored to them by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, and about this time the spirit of war and conquest seems to have taken hold of their servants in India, and never since to have left them. During the French war that began in 1755, their arms shared in the general good fortune of those of Great Britain. They defended Madras, took Pondicherry, recovered Calcutta, and acquired the revenues of a rich and extensive territory, amounting, it was then said, to upwards of three million a year. They remained for several years in quiet possession of this revenue; but in 1767 the administration laid claim to their territorial acquisitions, and the revenue arising from them, as of right belonging to the crown; and the company, in compensation for this claim, agreed to pay government £400,000 a year. Before this they had gradually raised their dividend from about six to ten per cent; that is, on their capital of three million two hundred thousand pounds they had increased it by £128,000, or raised it from one hundred and ninety-two thousand to three hundred and twenty thousand pounds a year. About this time they were attempting to raise it still further, to twelve and a half per cent, which would have made their annual payments to their proprietors equal to what they had agreed to pay government every year, or £400,000 a year. But during the two years in which their agreement with government was to take effect, they were restrained from any further increase of dividend by two successive acts of parliament, the aim of which was to enable them to make faster progress in paying off their debts, which were at this time estimated at upwards of six or seven million sterling. In 1769 they renewed their agreement with government for five years more, and stipulated that during that period they should be allowed gradually to raise their dividend to twelve and a half per cent, never increasing it, however, by more than one per cent in a year. So this increase of dividend, when it had risen to its utmost height, could add but £680,000 to their annual payments, to their proprietors and government together, beyond what they had been before their late territorial acquisitions. What the gross revenue of those territorial acquisitions was supposed to amount to has already been mentioned; and by an account brought by the Cruttenden East Indiaman in 1769, the net revenue, clear of all deductions and military charges, was put at two million forty-eight thousand seven hundred and forty-seven pounds. They were said at the same time to have another revenue, arising partly from lands but chiefly from the customs established at their various settlements, amounting to £439,000. The profits of their trade, too, according to the evidence of their chairman before the House of Commons, came at this time to at least £400,000 a year; according to that of their accountant, to at least £500,000; on the lowest account, at least equal to the highest dividend that was to be paid to their proprietors. So great a revenue might certainly have afforded an increase of £680,000 in their annual payments and, at the same time, have left a large sinking fund, enough for the speedy reduction of their debt. In 1773, however, their debts, instead of being reduced, were increased by an arrear to the Treasury in paying the four hundred thousand pounds; by another to the custom house for unpaid duties; by a large debt to the bank for money borrowed; and by a fourth, for bills drawn on them from India and recklessly accepted, to the amount of upwards of twelve hundred thousand pounds. The distress these accumulated claims brought on them obliged them not only to cut their dividend all at once to six per cent, but to throw themselves on the mercy of government, and to beg, first, a release from any further payment of the stipulated £400,000 a year, and second, a loan of fourteen hundred thousand to save them from immediate bankruptcy. The great increase of their fortune had, it seems, only served to furnish their servants with a pretext for greater extravagance, and a cover for greater malversation, than even in proportion to that increase of fortune. The conduct of their servants in India, and the general state of their affairs both in India and in Europe, became the subject of a parliamentary inquiry, in consequence of which several very important changes were made in the constitution of their government, both at home and abroad. In India, their principal settlements of Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta, which had before been wholly independent of one another, were placed under a governor-general assisted by a council of four assessors, parliament taking to itself the first nomination of this governor and council, who were to reside at Calcutta, that city having now become, what Madras had been before, the most important of the English settlements in India. The court of the Mayor of Calcutta, originally set up to try mercantile cases arising in the city and neighbourhood, had gradually extended its jurisdiction as the empire spread. It was now cut back and confined to the original purpose of its institution. In its place a new supreme court of judicature was established, consisting of a chief justice and three judges, to be appointed by the crown. In Europe, the qualification needed to entitle a proprietor to vote at their general courts was raised from five hundred pounds, the original price of a share in the company's stock, to a thousand pounds. To vote on this qualification, too, it was declared necessary that he should have held it, if acquired by his own purchase and not by inheritance, for at least one year, instead of the six months required before. The court of twenty-four directors had before been chosen annually; but it was now enacted that each director should in future be chosen for four years, six of them, however, to leave office by rotation every year, and not be eligible for re-election at the choosing of the six new directors for the following year. In consequence of these changes, the courts both of the proprietors and of the directors were expected to act with more dignity and steadiness than they usually had before. But it seems impossible, by any changes, to make those courts in any way fit to govern, or even to share in the government of, a great empire, because most of their members must always have too little interest in the prosperity of that empire to give any serious attention to what may promote it. Frequently a man of great fortune, sometimes even one of small fortune, is willing to buy a thousand-pound share in India stock merely for the influence he expects to gain by a vote in the court of proprietors. It gives him a share, not indeed in the plunder, but in the appointment of the plunderers of India; for the court of directors, though they make that appointment, are necessarily more or less under the influence of the proprietors, who not only elect those directors but sometimes overrule the appointments of their servants in India. Provided he can enjoy this influence for a few years, and thereby provide for a certain number of his friends, he frequently cares little about the dividend, or even about the value of the stock on which his vote is founded. About the prosperity of the great empire in whose government that vote gives him a share, he seldom cares at all. No other sovereigns ever were, or, from the nature of things, ever could be, so perfectly indifferent about the happiness or misery of their subjects, the improvement or waste of their dominions, the glory or disgrace of their administration, as, from irresistible moral causes, most of the proprietors of such a mercantile company are, and necessarily must be. This indifference, too, was more likely to be increased than lessened by some of the new regulations made in consequence of the parliamentary inquiry. By a resolution of the House of Commons, for example, it was declared that when the £1,400,000 lent to the company by government should be paid, and their bond debts reduced to £1,500,000, they might then, and not till then, divide eight per cent on their capital; and that whatever remained of their revenues and net profits at home should be divided into four parts, three of them to be paid into the Exchequer for the use of the public, and the fourth to be kept as a fund either for the further reduction of their bond debts or for meeting other contingent needs the company might labour under. But if the company were bad stewards and bad sovereigns when the whole of their net revenue and profits belonged to themselves and were at their own disposal, they were surely not likely to be better when three-fourths of it were to belong to other people, and the other fourth, though to be spent for the company's benefit, yet to be so under the inspection and with the approval of other people.

It might be more agreeable to the company that their own servants and dependants should have either the pleasure of wasting, or the profit of embezzling, whatever surplus remained after paying the proposed dividend of eight per cent, than that it should come into the hands of a set of people with whom those resolutions could scarcely fail to set them somewhat at odds. The interest of those servants and dependants might so far predominate in the court of proprietors as sometimes to dispose it to support the authors of depredations committed in direct violation of its own authority. For most of the proprietors, upholding even the authority of their own court might sometimes matter less than supporting those who had defied that authority.

The regulations of 1773 accordingly did not put an end to the disorder of the company's government in India. Even though, during a momentary fit of good conduct, they had at one time gathered into the treasury of Calcutta more than £3,000,000 sterling; even though they had afterwards extended either their dominion or their depredations over a vast addition of some of the richest and most fertile countries in India, all was wasted and destroyed. They found themselves wholly unprepared to stop or resist the incursion of Hyder Ali; and as a result of these disorders the company is now (1784) in greater distress than ever, and, to prevent immediate bankruptcy, is once more reduced to begging the assistance of government. Different plans have been proposed by the different parties in parliament for the better management of its affairs; and all those plans seem to agree in supposing, what was indeed always abundantly evident, that it is altogether unfit to govern its territorial possessions. Even the company itself seems convinced of its own incapacity in this, and seems on that account willing to hand them over to government.

With the right of holding forts and garrisons in distant and barbarous countries is necessarily connected the right of making peace and war in those countries. The joint-stock companies that have had the one right have constantly exercised the other, and have frequently had it expressly conferred on them. How unjustly, how capriciously, how cruelly they have commonly exercised it is too well known from recent experience.

When a company of merchants undertake, at their own risk and expense, to establish a new trade with some remote and barbarous nation, it may not be unreasonable to incorporate them into a joint-stock company and to grant them, if they succeed, a monopoly of the trade for a certain number of years. It is the easiest and most natural way in which the state can reward them for hazarding a dangerous and expensive experiment, of which the public is afterwards to reap the benefit. A temporary monopoly of this kind may be defended on the same principles on which a like monopoly of a new machine is granted to its inventor, and that of a new book to its author. But once the term expires, the monopoly ought certainly to end; the forts and garrisons, if any were found necessary to establish, should be taken into the hands of government, their value paid to the company, and the trade laid open to all the subjects of the state. By a perpetual monopoly, all the other subjects of the state are taxed very absurdly in two ways: first, by the high price of goods, which under free trade they could buy much cheaper; and second, by their total exclusion from a branch of business that it might be both convenient and profitable for many of them to carry on. And it is for the most worthless of all purposes that they are taxed in this way. It is merely to enable the company to support the negligence, extravagance, and malversation of their own servants, whose disorderly conduct seldom lets the company's dividend exceed the ordinary rate of profit in trades that are altogether free, and very frequently makes it fall even a good deal short of that rate. Without a monopoly, however, a joint-stock company, it would appear from experience, cannot long carry on any branch of foreign trade. To buy in one market in order to sell at a profit in another, when there are many competitors in both; to keep watch, not only over the occasional shifts in demand, but over the much greater and more frequent shifts in the competition, or in the supply that demand is likely to get from other people; and to suit, with skill and judgment, both the quantity and the quality of each assortment of goods to all these circumstances, is a species of warfare whose operations are continually changing, and which can scarcely ever be conducted successfully without such an unremitting exertion of vigilance and attention as cannot long be expected from the directors of a joint-stock company. The East India Company, on the redemption of their funds and the expiry of their exclusive privilege, have a right, by act of parliament, to continue as a corporation with a joint stock, and to trade in their corporate capacity to the East Indies in common with the rest of their fellow subjects. But in this situation the superior vigilance and attention of a private adventurer would, in all likelihood, soon make them weary of the trade.

A distinguished French writer with deep expertise in political economy, the Abbe Morellet, supplies a list of fifty-five joint-stock companies set up for foreign trade in various parts of Europe since the year 1600. By his account, every one of them collapsed through mismanagement, even though they all held exclusive privileges. He got the history of two or three of them wrong: those were not joint-stock companies and did not fail. But to balance that out, several joint-stock companies that did fail were left off his list.

The only trades a joint-stock company seems able to run successfully without an exclusive privilege are those whose every operation can be reduced to what we call a routine, or to a method so uniform that it varies little or not at all. There are four of these. The first is banking. The second is insurance against fire and against losses at sea, including capture in wartime. The third is building and maintaining a navigable channel or canal. The fourth, very similar, is bringing water to supply a large city.

The principles of banking may look rather obscure, but the practice can be reduced to strict rules. Breaking those rules on any occasion, tempted by some attractive prospect of unusual profit, is almost always extremely dangerous and often ruins the banking company that tries it. Joint-stock companies, by their very structure, tend to cling to established rules more stubbornly than any private partnership, so they are very well suited to this trade. That is why the leading banks in Europe are joint-stock companies, and many of them run their business very successfully with no exclusive privilege at all. The Bank of England holds no special privilege beyond this: no other banking company in England may have more than six partners. The two banks of Edinburgh are joint-stock companies with no exclusive privilege.

The value of a risk—whether from fire, from loss at sea, or from capture—may not be calculable with great precision, but it can be estimated roughly enough to bring it, to some degree, under strict rule and method. Insurance, therefore, can be carried on successfully by a joint-stock company without any exclusive privilege. Neither the London Assurance nor the Royal Exchange Assurance companies holds such a privilege.

Once a navigable channel or canal has been built, managing it becomes quite simple and easy and can be reduced to strict rule and method. Even the construction can be handled the same way, since it can be contracted out to undertakers at so much per mile and so much per lock. The same is true of a canal, an aqueduct, or a large pipe for supplying a great city with water. Projects like these therefore can be, and often are, run very successfully by joint-stock companies without any exclusive privilege.

Still, it would hardly be reasonable to set up a joint-stock company for some venture merely because such a company could manage it well, or to exempt a particular group of traders from the general laws that apply to all their neighbours merely because they might prosper given such an exemption. For such an arrangement to be fully justified, two further conditions, on top of the venture being reducible to strict rule and method, must both hold. First, it must be perfectly clear that the venture is of greater and more general usefulness than most ordinary trades. Second, it must require more capital than a private partnership could easily raise. If a modest amount of capital were enough, even great usefulness would not justify forming a joint-stock company, because in that case private entrepreneurs would readily meet the demand for whatever it produced. In the four trades named above, both conditions hold.

The great and general usefulness of banking, when it is managed prudently, was fully explained in the second book of this Inquiry. But a public bank that must underpin public credit and, in particular emergencies, advance the government the entire yield of a tax—perhaps several million pounds—a year or two before the money actually comes in, needs more capital than any private partnership could easily raise.

Insurance gives great security to private fortunes, and by spreading among many people a loss that would ruin one individual, it makes that loss fall lightly and easily on society as a whole. But to provide this security, the insurers must have a very large capital. It is said that before the two joint-stock insurance companies were set up in London, a list was presented to the attorney-general of one hundred and fifty private insurers who had gone bankrupt within a few years.

It is obvious enough that navigable channels and canals, together with the works sometimes needed to supply a great city with water, are of great and general usefulness while also often costing more than private fortunes can bear.

Apart from the four trades named above, I have not been able to think of any other in which all three conditions needed to justify a joint-stock company come together. The English copper company of London, the lead-smelting company, and the glass-grinding company cannot even claim any great or unusual usefulness in what they do; nor does what they do seem to require expense beyond the means of many private men. Whether the trade these companies carry on can be reduced to rules strict enough to suit a joint-stock company, and whether they have any grounds for boasting of unusual profits, I do not claim to know. The mine-adventurers company went bankrupt long ago. A share in the British Linen company of Edinburgh now sells well below par, though not as far below as it did some years ago. Joint-stock companies set up for the public-spirited aim of promoting some particular manufacture not only manage their own affairs badly, draining the general capital of society, but in other respects can scarcely ever fail to do more harm than good. However upright their intentions, their directors will inevitably favour particular branches of the manufacture about which the undertakers mislead and deceive them, and this discourages the rest. It necessarily disturbs, more or less, the natural proportion that would otherwise settle between sensible enterprise and profit—a proportion that is, of all encouragements to a country's general industry, the greatest and most effective.
Article II: The Expense of Institutions for the Education of Youth.
Institutions for educating the young can, in the same way, generate enough income to cover their own costs. The fee or honorarium that a pupil pays the teacher naturally provides income of this kind.

Even where the teacher's reward does not come entirely from this natural income, there is still no need for it to be drawn from the society's general revenue, the collection and disposal of which is in most countries handed to the executive power. Across most of Europe, in fact, endowing schools and colleges places either no burden at all on that general revenue, or only a very small one. Almost everywhere the funding comes chiefly from some local or provincial source—the rent of a landed estate, or the interest on a sum of money set aside and placed under trustees for this particular purpose, sometimes by the sovereign himself and sometimes by a private donor.

Have these public endowments, on the whole, advanced the aim for which they were founded? Have they encouraged teachers to work hard and improve their abilities? Have they steered education toward subjects more useful, both to the individual and to the public, than it would have moved toward on its own? It should not be very hard to give at least a likely answer to each of these questions.

In every profession, how hard most of its members work is always proportional to how badly they need to work hard. That need is greatest for those whose only expected source of fortune—or even of ordinary income and subsistence—is what their profession earns them. To gain that fortune, or merely to make a living, they must each year do a certain amount of work of recognised value; and where competition is free, the rivalry of competitors all trying to push one another out of work forces every man to do his own with a certain degree of care. The size of the prizes won by success in some particular professions may, no doubt, sometimes spur on a few men of extraordinary spirit and ambition. But great prizes are clearly not necessary to produce the greatest effort. Rivalry and emulation make excellence an object of ambition even in lowly professions, and often produce the greatest effort of all. Great prizes, by contrast, standing alone and unsupported by any necessity to apply oneself, have rarely been enough to produce much effort. In England, success at the law leads to some very great objects of ambition; and yet how few men born to comfortable fortunes have ever been distinguished in that profession in this country?

Endowing schools and colleges has inevitably reduced, to a greater or lesser degree, the teachers' need to apply themselves. Their livelihood, so far as it comes from their salaries, plainly comes from a fund that is entirely independent of their success and reputation in their particular field.

At some universities the salary is only part, and often only a small part, of the teacher's earnings, most of which comes from the honoraria or fees paid by his pupils. Here the need to apply oneself, though always reduced to some degree, is not entirely removed. Reputation in his field still matters to him, and he still depends to some extent on the affection, gratitude, and good word of those who have attended his teaching; and the surest way to win those favourable feelings is to deserve them—that is, through the ability and diligence with which he carries out every part of his duty.

At other universities the teacher is forbidden to take any honorarium or fee from his pupils, and his salary is the whole of the income he draws from his post. Here his interest is set as squarely against his duty as it can possibly be. Every man's interest is to live as comfortably as he can; and if his earnings will be exactly the same whether or not he performs some very laborious duty, then his interest—at least as interest is commonly understood—is either to neglect that duty altogether, or, if he is under some authority that will not permit this, to perform it as carelessly and sloppily as that authority will allow. If he happens to be naturally active and fond of work, his interest is to spend that energy in some pursuit from which he can gain an advantage rather than in his duty, which yields him none.

Suppose the authority over him rests with the corporate body—the college or university—of which he is himself a member, and most of the other members are, like him, people who either are teachers or ought to be. They are likely to make common cause, to be very lenient with one another, and for each to agree that his neighbour may neglect his duty provided he himself is allowed to neglect his own. At the University of Oxford, most of the public professors have, for many years now, given up even the pretence of teaching.

Suppose instead that the authority over him rests not so much with the corporate body of which he is a member but with some outside party—the bishop of the diocese, say, or the provincial governor, or perhaps some minister of state. In that case he is not very likely to be allowed to neglect his duty altogether. But all such superiors can compel him to do is attend his pupils for a set number of hours—that is, deliver a set number of lectures each week or each year. What those lectures actually contain still depends on the teacher's diligence, and that diligence is likely to match the motives he has for exerting it. An outside jurisdiction of this kind, moreover, is liable to be exercised both ignorantly and capriciously. By its very nature it is arbitrary and discretionary; and the people who wield it, neither attending the teacher's lectures themselves nor perhaps even understanding the subjects he is meant to teach, are rarely able to wield it with good judgment. Out of the arrogance of office, too, they are often indifferent about how they use it, and very ready to censure him or strip him of his post wantonly and without any just cause. A person under such jurisdiction is inevitably degraded by it, and instead of being one of the most respected members of society he becomes one of the lowest and most contemptible. Only through powerful patronage can he effectively shield himself from the ill-treatment to which he is always exposed; and he is most likely to win that patronage not through ability or diligence in his profession, but through fawning compliance with his superiors' wishes, and through being ready at all times to sacrifice to that will the rights, the interests, and the honour of the corporate body of which he is a member. Anyone who has watched the running of a French university for any length of time must have had occasion to note the effects that naturally flow from an arbitrary, outside jurisdiction of this kind.

Anything that forces a certain number of students into a particular college or university, regardless of the teachers' merit or reputation, tends to some degree to reduce the need for that merit or reputation.

The privileges of graduates in arts, law, medicine, and divinity, when they can be obtained only by residing a certain number of years at certain universities, necessarily force a certain number of students into those universities regardless of the teachers' merit or reputation. The privileges of graduates are a kind of apprenticeship statute, and they have done as much to improve education as the other apprenticeship statutes have done to improve the arts and manufactures.

The charitable foundations of scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries, and the like necessarily tie a certain number of students to certain colleges, regardless of the merit of those particular colleges. If students on such charitable foundations were left free to choose whichever college they liked best, that freedom might perhaps stir up some rivalry among different colleges. A rule of the opposite kind, forbidding even the independent members of a particular college to leave it for another without first asking and obtaining the permission of the one they meant to leave, would do a great deal to stifle that rivalry.

Suppose that in each college the tutor or teacher assigned to instruct each student in all arts and sciences were not freely chosen by the student but appointed by the head of the college; and suppose that, in cases of neglect, incompetence, or mistreatment, the student were not allowed to switch to another tutor without first asking and obtaining permission. Such a rule would not only do much to stifle all rivalry among the various tutors of the same college, but would also greatly reduce, in all of them, the need for diligence and attention to their pupils. Teachers like these, though well paid by their students, might be just as inclined to neglect them as those who are not paid by their students at all, or who get nothing but their salary.

If the teacher happens to be a man of sense, it must be unpleasant for him to know, while lecturing to his students, that he is either speaking or reading nonsense, or something little better than nonsense. It must also be unpleasant to see that most of his students stay away from his lectures, or perhaps attend with clear signs of neglect, contempt, and ridicule. So if he is required to give a set number of lectures, these motives alone, with no other interest at stake, might lead him to take some trouble to make them tolerably good. There are, however, several devices he can resort to that will effectively dull the edge of all these spurs to diligence. Instead of explaining the subject to his pupils himself, the teacher may simply read some book on it; and if that book is in a foreign and dead language, he can interpret it for them into their own tongue—or, with even less effort, have them interpret it to him—and, by adding the occasional remark here and there, flatter himself that he is giving a lecture. The slightest knowledge and effort will let him do this without exposing himself to contempt or ridicule by saying anything truly foolish, absurd, or ridiculous. The discipline of the college, meanwhile, may let him compel all his pupils to attend this sham lecture most regularly, and to keep up the most decent and respectful behaviour throughout the whole performance.

The discipline of colleges and universities is generally designed not for the benefit of the students but for the interest—or, more accurately, the ease—of the masters. Its aim, in every case, is to uphold the master's authority and, whether he neglects or performs his duty, to make the students treat him in every case as though he carried it out with the greatest diligence and ability. It seems to assume perfect wisdom and virtue in the one group, and the greatest weakness and folly in the other. Yet where the masters really do perform their duty, I believe there are no cases in which most of the students ever neglect theirs. No discipline is ever needed to compel attendance at lectures that are genuinely worth attending, as everyone knows wherever such lectures are given.
