Force and restraint may, no doubt, be somewhat necessary to make children or very young boys attend to the parts of education thought necessary for them to acquire at that early stage of life; but after the age of twelve or thirteen, provided the master does his duty, force or restraint can hardly ever be needed to carry on any part of education. Such is the generosity of most young men that, far from being inclined to neglect or scorn their master's teaching, provided he shows some serious intention of being useful to them, they are generally ready to forgive a great deal of imperfection in his performance of his duty, and sometimes even to hide from the public a great deal of gross negligence.

It is worth noting that the parts of education for which there are no public institutions are generally the best taught. When a young man goes to a fencing or dancing school, he does not always learn to fence or dance very well, but he seldom fails to learn to fence or dance at all. The good effects of the riding school are not usually as plain. A riding school is so expensive that in most places it is a public institution. The three most essential parts of a literary education—reading, writing, and accounting—are still more commonly acquired in private than in public schools; and it very rarely happens that anyone fails to acquire them to the degree in which they need to be acquired.

In England the public schools are far less corrupted than the universities. In the schools the youth are taught, or at least may be taught, Greek and Latin—that is, everything the masters claim to teach, or are expected to teach. In the universities the youth are neither taught, nor can always find any proper means of being taught, the sciences which it is the very business of those corporate bodies to teach. The schoolmaster's reward, in most cases, depends mainly—and in some cases almost entirely—on the fees or honoraria of his pupils. Schools have no exclusive privileges. To win the honours of graduation, a person need not produce a certificate proving he has studied a certain number of years at a public school. If, on examination, he appears to understand what is taught there, no questions are asked about where he learned it.

It may perhaps be said that the parts of education commonly taught in universities are not very well taught. But without those institutions they would not have been commonly taught at all, and both the individual and the public would have suffered a good deal from the lack of those important parts of education.

Most of the present universities of Europe were originally ecclesiastical corporations set up to educate churchmen. They were founded by the pope's authority and stood so entirely under his immediate protection that their members, whether masters or students, all enjoyed what was then called the benefit of clergy—that is, they were exempt from the civil jurisdiction of the countries where their universities stood and were answerable only to the ecclesiastical courts. What was taught in most of these universities suited the aim for which they were founded: either theology, or something merely preparatory to theology.

When Christianity was first established by law, a corrupted form of Latin had become the common language of all the western parts of Europe. The church service, accordingly, and the translation of the Bible read in churches, were both in that corrupted Latin—that is, in the common language of the country. After the inrush of the barbarous nations that overturned the Roman empire, Latin gradually ceased to be the language of any part of Europe. But people's reverence naturally preserves the established forms and ceremonies of religion long after the circumstances that first introduced them and made them reasonable have disappeared. So although Latin was no longer understood anywhere by the bulk of the people, the whole church service still went on being performed in that language. Two distinct languages thus became established in Europe, just as in ancient Egypt: a language of the priests and a language of the people, a sacred and a profane, a learned and an unlearned tongue. But the priests had to understand something of the sacred and learned language in which they were to officiate, and so the study of Latin made up, from the very beginning, an essential part of university education.

It was not so with either Greek or Hebrew. The infallible decrees of the church had declared the Latin translation of the Bible, commonly called the Latin Vulgate, to have been dictated by divine inspiration just as the Greek and Hebrew originals were, and therefore to carry equal authority with them. Since knowledge of those two languages was thus not strictly necessary for a churchman, studying them did not, for a long time, form a necessary part of the ordinary university course. There are some Spanish universities, I am assured, where the study of Greek has never yet formed any part of that course. The first reformers found the Greek text of the New Testament, and even the Hebrew text of the Old, more favourable to their views than the Vulgate translation, which, as one might naturally expect, had been gradually adjusted to support the doctrines of the Catholic Church. They therefore set out to expose the many errors of that translation, which the Roman Catholic clergy were thus forced to defend or explain. But this could not well be done without some knowledge of the original languages, and so their study was gradually brought into most universities, both those that embraced and those that rejected the doctrines of the Reformation. Greek was bound up with every part of that classical learning which, though first cultivated chiefly by Catholics and Italians, happened to come into fashion at about the same time the doctrines of the Reformation were launched. In most universities, therefore, Greek was taught before the study of philosophy, as soon as the student had made some progress in Latin. Hebrew, having no connection with classical learning and being—apart from the Holy Scriptures—the language of not a single book held in any esteem, was not usually begun until after philosophy, once the student had taken up the study of theology.

Originally the first rudiments of both Greek and Latin were taught in the universities, and in some universities they still are. In others, the student is expected to have already acquired at least the rudiments of one or both of those languages, the study of which still everywhere makes up a very considerable part of university education.

Ancient Greek philosophy was divided into three great branches: physics, or natural philosophy; ethics, or moral philosophy; and logic. This general division seems perfectly suited to the nature of things.

The great phenomena of nature—the movements of the heavenly bodies, eclipses, comets, thunder and lightning and other extraordinary atmospheric events, and the generation, life, growth, and dissolution of plants and animals—are things that, just as they necessarily provoke wonder, naturally rouse mankind's curiosity to inquire into their causes. Superstition first tried to satisfy this curiosity by tracing all these wonderful appearances to the direct action of the gods. Philosophy afterwards tried to explain them by more familiar causes, or by ones mankind knew better than the action of the gods. Since these great phenomena are the first objects of human curiosity, the science claiming to explain them must naturally have been the first branch of philosophy to be cultivated. Accordingly, the first philosophers of whom history has preserved any record appear to have been natural philosophers.

In every age and country of the world, people must have paid attention to one another's characters, intentions, and actions, and many respectable rules and maxims for the conduct of human life must have been laid down and approved by common consent. As soon as writing came into fashion, wise men—or those who fancied themselves such—would naturally try to add to the stock of these established and respected maxims, and to set down their own sense of what counted as proper or improper conduct, sometimes in the more elaborate form of fables, like those called the fables of Aesop, and sometimes in the simpler form of apophthegms or wise sayings, like the proverbs of Solomon, the verses of Theognis and Phocyllides, and part of the works of Hesiod. They might go on this way for a long time, merely multiplying the number of these maxims of prudence and morality, without even trying to arrange them in any very distinct or methodical order, much less to link them together under one or more general principles from which they could all be derived, like effects from their natural causes. The beauty of arranging different observations systematically, connected by a few common principles, was first glimpsed in those crude early attempts at a system of natural philosophy. Something of the same kind was afterwards attempted in morals. The maxims of everyday life were set in some methodical order and tied together by a few common principles, just as people had tried to arrange and connect the phenomena of nature. The science that claims to investigate and explain these connecting principles is what is properly called Moral Philosophy.

Different authors offered different systems of both natural and moral philosophy. But the arguments by which they supported these systems, far from always being demonstrations, were often at best only very slender probabilities, and sometimes mere sophistries with no foundation beyond the inaccuracy and ambiguity of everyday language. In every age of the world, speculative systems have been adopted for reasons too trivial to have swayed the judgment of any sensible man in a matter involving the smallest sum of money. Crude sophistry has scarcely ever had any influence on mankind's opinions except in matters of philosophy and speculation, and in those it has often had the greatest influence. The champions of each system of natural and moral philosophy naturally tried to expose the weakness of the arguments offered in support of the rival systems. In examining those arguments, they were necessarily led to consider the difference between a probable and a demonstrative argument, between a fallacious one and a conclusive one; and logic, the science of the general principles of good and bad reasoning, necessarily grew out of the observations to which such scrutiny gave rise. Although in its origin logic came after both physics and ethics, it was commonly taught—not in all, but in most of the ancient schools of philosophy—before either of those sciences. The student, it seems to have been thought, ought to understand clearly the difference between good and bad reasoning before he was set to reason on subjects of such great importance.
In most of the universities of Europe, this ancient division of philosophy into three parts was replaced by another into five.

In the ancient philosophy, everything taught about the nature of either the human mind or the Deity formed part of the system of physics. Those beings, whatever their essence was supposed to be, were parts of the great system of the universe, and parts that produced the most important effects. Whatever human reason could conclude or conjecture about them made up, as it were, two chapters—two very important ones, no doubt—of the science that claimed to account for the origin and movements of the great system of the universe. But in the universities of Europe, where philosophy was taught only as a servant to theology, it was natural to dwell longer on these two chapters than on any other part of the science. They were gradually expanded more and more and split into many lesser chapters, until at last the doctrine of spirits, about which so little can be known, came to take up as much room in the system of philosophy as the doctrine of bodies, about which so much can be known. The doctrines on these two subjects were treated as forming two distinct sciences. What is called metaphysics, or pneumatics, was set against physics and cultivated not only as the loftier science of the two but, for the purposes of a particular profession, as the more useful one. The proper subject of experiment and observation—a subject in which careful attention can make so many useful discoveries—was almost entirely neglected. The subject in which, after a very few simple and almost obvious truths, the most careful attention can find nothing but obscurity and uncertainty, and so can produce nothing but subtleties and sophistries, was cultivated to a great degree.

Once these two sciences had been set against each other, comparing them naturally gave rise to a third, called ontology, the science that dealt with the qualities and attributes common to the subjects of the other two. But if subtleties and sophistries made up most of the metaphysics or pneumatics of the schools, they made up the whole of this cobweb science of ontology, which was likewise sometimes called metaphysics.

What constituted the happiness and perfection of a man—considered not only as an individual but as a member of a family, of a state, and of the great society of mankind—was the question that ancient moral philosophy set out to investigate. In that philosophy, the duties of human life were treated as a means to the happiness and perfection of human life. But once moral philosophy, like natural philosophy, came to be taught only as a servant to theology, the duties of human life were treated as chiefly a means to the happiness of a life to come. In the ancient philosophy, perfect virtue was presented as necessarily producing, for the person who possessed it, the most perfect happiness in this life. In the modern philosophy, it was often presented as generally—indeed almost always—incompatible with any degree of happiness in this life; heaven was to be earned only by penance and mortification, by the austerities and self-abasement of a monk, not by the generous, high-minded, and spirited conduct of a man. Casuistry and an ascetic morality made up, in most cases, the greater part of the schools' moral philosophy. The single most important branch of all philosophy thus became by far the most corrupted.

Such, then, was the usual course of philosophical education in most of the universities of Europe. Logic was taught first; ontology came second; pneumatology—covering the doctrine of the nature of the human soul and of the Deity—came third; fourth came a debased system of moral philosophy, regarded as directly tied to the doctrines of pneumatology, to the immortality of the human soul, and to the rewards and punishments that, from the justice of the Deity, were to be expected in a life to come; and a short and superficial system of physics usually closed the course.

The changes that the universities of Europe introduced into the ancient course of philosophy were all aimed at educating clergymen and at making philosophy a more fitting introduction to the study of theology. But the extra subtlety and sophistry, the casuistry and ascetic morality those changes brought into it certainly did not make it more suitable for educating gentlemen or men of the world, nor more likely either to improve the understanding or to mend the heart.

This course of philosophy is what still goes on being taught in most of the universities of Europe, with more or less diligence depending on how far each particular university's constitution happens to make diligence necessary for its teachers. In some of the richest and best-endowed universities, the tutors content themselves with teaching a few unconnected scraps of this corrupted course, and even those they commonly teach very carelessly and superficially.

Most of the improvements made in modern times in the various branches of philosophy have not been made in universities, though some, no doubt, have. Most universities have not even been quick to adopt those improvements once they were made; and several of these learned societies have chosen to remain, for a long time, the sanctuaries in which discredited systems and obsolete prejudices found shelter and protection after they had been driven out of every other corner of the world. In general, the richest and best-endowed universities have been the slowest to adopt those improvements and the most resistant to any considerable change in the established plan of education. Those improvements were more easily introduced into some of the poorer universities, where the teachers, depending on their reputation for most of their livelihood, were obliged to pay more attention to the current opinions of the world.

Although the public schools and universities of Europe were originally meant only to educate one particular profession, that of churchmen—and although they were not always very diligent even in teaching their pupils the sciences supposed necessary for that profession—they gradually drew to themselves the education of nearly everyone else, particularly of almost all gentlemen and men of fortune. No better way, it seems, could be found of spending to any advantage the long interval between infancy and the age at which men begin to apply themselves in earnest to the real business of the world, the business that is to occupy them for the rest of their days. Yet most of what is taught in schools and universities does not seem to be the most fitting preparation for that business.

In England it becomes more and more the custom every day to send young people travelling in foreign countries as soon as they leave school, without sending them to any university. Our young people, it is said, generally come home much improved by their travels. A young man who goes abroad at seventeen or eighteen and comes home at twenty-one returns three or four years older than when he left; and at that age it is very hard not to improve a good deal in three or four years. In the course of his travels he generally picks up some knowledge of one or two foreign languages—though seldom enough to let him speak or write them properly. In other respects he commonly comes home more conceited, more unprincipled, more dissipated, and less capable of any serious application to study or business than he could well have become in so short a time had he stayed at home. By travelling so very young, by squandering the most precious years of his life in the most frivolous dissipation, far from the watch and control of his parents and relations, every useful habit that the earlier parts of his education might have begun to form in him—instead of being fixed and confirmed—is almost inevitably weakened or wiped out. Nothing but the disrepute into which the universities are letting themselves fall could ever have brought into fashion so absurd a practice as travelling at this early period of life. By sending his son abroad, a father relieves himself, at least for a time, of so disagreeable a sight as that of a son idle, neglected, and going to ruin before his eyes.
Such have been the effects of some of the modern institutions for education.
Different plans and different institutions for education seem to have existed in other ages and nations.

In the republics of ancient Greece, every free citizen was instructed, under the direction of the public magistrate, in gymnastic exercises and in music. The aim of the gymnastic exercises was to toughen his body, sharpen his courage, and prepare him for the hardships and dangers of war; and since the Greek militia was, by all accounts, one of the best the world has ever seen, this part of their public education must have served its intended purpose completely. The aim of the other part, music—at least according to the philosophers and historians who have left us an account of these institutions—was to civilise the mind, soften the temper, and dispose it to perform all the social and moral duties of public and private life.

In ancient Rome, the exercises of the Campus Martius served the same purpose as those of the Gymnasium in ancient Greece, and they seem to have served it equally well. But among the Romans there was nothing corresponding to the musical education of the Greeks. Even so, the morals of the Romans, in both private and public life, seem to have been not merely equal but, on the whole, a good deal superior to those of the Greeks. That they were superior in private life we have on the express testimony of Polybius and of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, two authors well acquainted with both nations; and the whole course of Greek and Roman history bears witness to the superiority of Roman public morals. The good temper and moderation of rival factions seem to be the most essential feature of the public morals of a free people. But the factions of the Greeks were almost always violent and bloody, whereas until the time of the Gracchi no blood had ever been shed in any Roman faction; and from the time of the Gracchi the Roman republic may be regarded as in reality dissolved. So, despite the very respectable authority of Plato, Aristotle, and Polybius, and despite the very ingenious reasons by which Montesquieu tries to support that authority, it seems likely that the musical education of the Greeks did little to improve their morals, since without any such education those of the Romans were, on the whole, superior. The respect of those ancient sages for the institutions of their ancestors had probably inclined them to find much political wisdom in what was perhaps merely an ancient custom, carried on without interruption from the earliest period of those societies down to the times when they had reached a considerable degree of refinement. Music and dancing are the great amusements of almost all barbarous nations, and the great accomplishments thought to fit a man for entertaining his company. It is so to this day among the negroes on the coast of Africa. It was so among the ancient Celts, among the ancient Scandinavians, and, as we learn from Homer, among the ancient Greeks in the times before the Trojan war. When the Greek tribes had formed themselves into little republics, it was natural that the study of these accomplishments should for a long time form part of the public and common education of the people.

The masters who instructed the young people in music or in military exercises do not seem to have been paid, or even appointed, by the state, either in Rome or even at Athens, the Greek republic whose laws and customs we know best. The state required every free citizen to fit himself for defending it in war and, for that reason, to learn his military exercises. But it left him to learn them from whatever masters he could find, and it seems to have provided nothing for this purpose but a public field or exercise ground where he could practise and perform them.

In the early ages of both the Greek and Roman republics, the rest of education seems to have consisted in learning to read, write, and account according to the arithmetic of the times. The richer citizens seem often to have acquired these accomplishments at home, with the help of a household tutor who was generally either a slave or a freedman; the poorer citizens learned them in the schools of such masters as made a trade of teaching for hire. Even so, these parts of education were left entirely to the care of each individual's parents or guardians. The state does not appear ever to have taken on any inspection or direction of them. By a law of Solon, indeed, children were released from any duty to support parents who had neglected to have them taught some profitable trade or business.

As refinement advanced and philosophy and rhetoric came into fashion, the better sort of people would send their children to the schools of philosophers and rhetoricians to be instructed in these fashionable subjects. But those schools were not supported by the public; for a long time they were barely tolerated by it. The demand for philosophy and rhetoric was for a long time so small that the first professional teachers of either could not find steady employment in any one city and were obliged to travel from place to place. This was how Zeno of Elea, Protagoras, Gorgias, Hippias, and many others lived. As demand grew, the schools of both philosophy and rhetoric settled in one place, first in Athens and afterwards in several other cities. The state, however, seems never to have encouraged them beyond assigning some of them a particular place to teach in—something that was sometimes done by private donors as well. The state seems to have assigned the Academy to Plato, the Lyceum to Aristotle, and the Portico to Zeno of Citium, the founder of the Stoics. But Epicurus left his gardens to his own school. Until about the time of Marcus Antoninus, however, no teacher appears to have drawn any salary from the public or to have had any earnings beyond the honoraria or fees of his pupils. The bounty that this philosophical emperor, as we learn from Lucian, bestowed on one of the teachers of philosophy probably lasted no longer than his own life. There was nothing equivalent to the privileges of graduation, and attending any of these schools was not required in order to practise any particular trade or profession. If the belief in their own usefulness could not draw students to them, the law neither forced anyone to attend them nor rewarded anyone for having done so. The teachers had no jurisdiction over their pupils and no authority beyond the natural authority that superior virtue and ability never fail to win from young people toward those entrusted with any part of their education.

At Rome, the study of the civil law formed part of the education not of most citizens but of certain particular families. The young people who wished to gain knowledge of the law had no public school to go to, and no way of studying it except by keeping company with such of their relations and friends as were supposed to understand it. It is perhaps worth remarking that, although many of the laws of the twelve tables were copied from those of some ancient Greek republics, law never seems to have grown into a science in any republic of ancient Greece. At Rome it became a science very early, and gave a considerable degree of distinction to those citizens who had a reputation for understanding it. In the republics of ancient Greece, particularly in Athens, the ordinary courts of justice consisted of numerous—and therefore disorderly—bodies of people, who often decided almost at random, or as clamour, faction, and party spirit happened to dictate. The disgrace of an unjust decision, when it was shared among five hundred, a thousand, or fifteen hundred people—for some of their courts were that large—could not fall very heavily on any one person. At Rome, by contrast, the principal courts of justice consisted either of a single judge or of a small number of judges, whose reputations, especially since they always deliberated in public, could not fail to be badly affected by any rash or unjust decision. In doubtful cases such courts, anxious to avoid blame, would naturally try to shelter behind the example or precedent of the judges who had sat before them, whether in the same court or in some other. This attention to practice and precedent necessarily shaped Roman law into the regular and orderly system in which it has been handed down to us; and the same attention has had the same effects on the laws of every other country where it has been applied. The superiority of character in the Romans over the Greeks, so often remarked by Polybius and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, was probably owing more to the better constitution of their courts of justice than to any of the circumstances to which those authors attribute it. The Romans are said to have been especially distinguished for their superior respect for an oath. But people who were used to swearing only before some diligent and well-informed court of justice would naturally be far more careful about what they swore than those who were used to doing the same thing before mobbish and disorderly assemblies.

The abilities, both civil and military, of the Greeks and Romans will readily be granted to have been at least equal to those of any modern nation. Our prejudice is perhaps rather to overrate them. But except in matters relating to military exercises, the state seems to have taken no trouble to form those great abilities; for I cannot bring myself to believe that the musical education of the Greeks could have done much to form them. Masters had nonetheless been found, it seems, to instruct the better sort of people among those nations in every art and science that the circumstances of their society made it necessary or convenient for them to learn. The demand for such instruction produced, as it always does, the talent for giving it; and the emulation that an unrestrained competition never fails to excite seems to have brought that talent to a very high degree of perfection. In the attention that the ancient philosophers commanded, in the hold they gained over the opinions and principles of their listeners, and in their power to give a certain tone and character to the conduct and conversation of those listeners, they appear to have been far superior to any modern teachers. In modern times, the diligence of public teachers is corrupted, more or less, by the very circumstances that make them more or less independent of their success and reputation in their particular fields. Their salaries, too, put the private teacher who would try to compete with them in the position of a merchant who tries to trade without a bounty against rivals who trade with a substantial one. If he sells his goods at nearly the same price, he cannot make the same profit, and poverty and destitution at least, if not bankruptcy and ruin, will inevitably be his lot. If he tries to sell them much dearer, he is likely to have so few customers that his situation will not be much improved. Besides, in many countries the privileges of graduation are necessary, or at least extremely convenient, to most men in the learned professions—that is, to by far the greater part of those who need a learned education. But those privileges can be obtained only by attending the lectures of the public teachers. The most careful attendance on the ablest instruction of any private teacher can never by itself entitle a man to demand them. From all these different causes, the private teacher of any of the sciences commonly taught in universities is, in modern times, generally regarded as belonging to the very lowest rank of men of letters. A man of real ability can scarcely find a more humiliating or less profitable employment for his talents. The endowments of schools and colleges have in this way not only corrupted the diligence of public teachers but have made it almost impossible to have any good private ones.

Were there no public institutions for education, no system and no science would be taught for which there was not some demand, or which the circumstances of the times did not make either necessary, or convenient, or at least fashionable to learn. A private teacher could never find it worth his while to teach either a discredited and antiquated version of a science admitted to be useful, or a science universally believed to be a mere useless and pedantic heap of sophistry and nonsense. Such systems and such sciences can survive nowhere but in those incorporated societies for education whose prosperity and revenue are largely independent of their own industry. Were there no public institutions for education, a gentleman who had gone through, with diligence and ability, the most complete course of education the circumstances of the times were thought to afford could not come into the world entirely ignorant of everything that is the common subject of conversation among gentlemen and men of the world.

There are no public institutions for the education of women, and so there is nothing useless, absurd, or fanciful in the usual course of their education. They are taught whatever their parents or guardians judge it necessary or useful for them to learn, and nothing else. Every part of their education plainly serves some useful purpose: either to enhance the natural attractions of their person, or to form their mind to reserve, modesty, chastity, and economy—to make them both likely to become the mistress of a family and able to behave properly once they have become one. In every part of her life a woman feels some convenience or advantage from every part of her education. It seldom happens that a man, in any part of his life, derives any convenience or advantage from some of the most laborious and troublesome parts of his education.

Ought the public, then, it may be asked, to pay no attention to the education of the people? Or, if it ought to pay some, which parts of education ought it to attend to in the different ranks of the people, and in what manner ought it to attend to them?

In some cases, the state of society naturally places most individuals in situations that form in them, with no help from government, almost all the abilities and virtues that state requires, or perhaps can admit of. In other cases, the state of society does not place most individuals in such situations, and some attention from government is needed to prevent the almost total corruption and degeneracy of the great body of the people.

As the division of labour advances, the work of the vast majority of those who live by labour—that is, of the great body of the people—comes to be confined to a few very simple operations, often to just one or two. But the understandings of most men are necessarily formed by their ordinary occupations. A man whose whole life is spent performing a few simple operations, whose effects too are perhaps always the same or very nearly so, has no occasion to exert his understanding or use his invention in finding ways around difficulties that never arise. He naturally loses the habit of such exertion, and generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human being to become. The numbness of his mind makes him not only unable to enjoy or take part in any rational conversation, but unable to feel any generous, noble, or tender sentiment, and so unable to form any sound judgment even about many of the ordinary duties of private life. Of the great and far-reaching interests of his country he is altogether incapable of judging; and unless very particular pains have been taken to make him otherwise, he is just as incapable of defending his country in war. The sameness of his settled life naturally corrupts the courage of his mind and makes him regard with horror the irregular, uncertain, and adventurous life of a soldier. It corrupts even the activity of his body and leaves him unable to exert his strength with vigour and perseverance in any occupation other than the one he was bred to. His skill at his own particular trade thus seems to be acquired at the expense of his intellectual, social, and martial virtues. But in every improved and civilised society this is the state into which the labouring poor—that is, the great body of the people—must necessarily fall, unless the government takes some pains to prevent it.

It is otherwise in the so-called barbarous societies of hunters, of shepherds, and even of husbandmen in that rude state of agriculture that comes before the rise of manufactures and the spread of foreign commerce. In such societies, the varied occupations of every man force every man to exert his capacity and to invent ways around the difficulties that continually arise. Invention is kept alive, and the mind is not allowed to sink into that drowsy stupidity which, in a civilised society, seems to numb the understanding of almost all the lower ranks of people. In those so-called barbarous societies, every man, as has already been observed, is a warrior. Every man too is in some degree a statesman, and can form a tolerable judgment about the interest of the society and the conduct of those who govern it. How far their chiefs are good judges in peace or good leaders in war is plain to the observation of almost every single man among them. In such a society, to be sure, no man can readily acquire the improved and refined understanding that a few men sometimes possess in a more civilised state. Although in a rude society there is a good deal of variety in the occupations of each individual, there is not much variety in those of the whole society. Every man does, or is capable of doing, almost everything that any other man does or is capable of doing. Every man has a considerable degree of knowledge, ingenuity, and invention, but scarcely any man has a great degree of it. The degree commonly possessed is generally enough for conducting the whole simple business of the society. In a civilised state, by contrast, although there is little variety in the occupations of most individuals, there is an almost infinite variety in those of the whole society. These varied occupations present an almost infinite variety of objects for the contemplation of those few who, being tied to no particular occupation themselves, have the leisure and the inclination to examine the occupations of others. The contemplation of so great a variety of objects necessarily exercises their minds in endless comparisons and combinations, and makes their understandings, to an extraordinary degree, both sharp and comprehensive. Yet unless those few happen to be placed in some very particular situations, their great abilities, however creditable to themselves, may contribute very little to the good government or happiness of their society. For all the great abilities of those few, all the nobler parts of the human character may be, to a great extent, blotted out and extinguished in the great body of the people.

In a civilised and commercial society, the education of the common people requires the attention of the public perhaps more than that of people of some rank and fortune. People of some rank and fortune are generally eighteen or nineteen years old before they take up the particular business, profession, or trade by which they mean to distinguish themselves in the world. Before then they have ample time to acquire, or at least to prepare themselves for afterwards acquiring, every accomplishment that can win them public esteem or make them worthy of it. Their parents or guardians are generally anxious enough that they should be so accomplished, and in most cases willing enough to lay out the necessary expense. If they are not always properly educated, it is seldom for lack of money spent on their education, but rather from spending it badly. It is seldom for lack of masters, but rather from the negligence and incapacity of the masters to be had, and from the difficulty—or rather the impossibility—of finding any better in the present state of things. The employments, too, in which people of some rank or fortune spend most of their lives are not, like those of the common people, simple and uniform. Almost all of them are extremely complicated and exercise the head more than the hands. The understandings of those engaged in such employments can seldom grow numb for want of exercise. Besides, the employments of people of some rank and fortune are seldom such as to wear them out from morning to night. They generally have a good deal of leisure, during which they may perfect themselves in every branch of useful or ornamental knowledge whose foundation they may have laid, or for which they may have acquired some taste, in the earlier part of life.

Things are different for ordinary people. They have hardly any time to spare for education. Their parents can barely afford to keep them, even in childhood. As soon as the children are able to work, they must take up some trade that lets them earn a living. And that trade is usually so simple and repetitive that it gives the mind little to do, while the work itself is so constant and so hard that it leaves them little leisure, and even less desire, to take up or even think about anything else.

It is true that, in any civilised society, ordinary people cannot be educated as thoroughly as those with some rank and money. Still, the most essential parts of education—reading, writing, and arithmetic—can be picked up so early in life that even most of those destined for the lowest occupations have time to learn them before they start working. At a very small cost, the public can make this learning easier, can encourage it, and can even require almost the entire population to acquire these most essential parts of an education.

The public can make this learning easier by setting up a small school in every parish or district, where children can be taught for a fee so modest that even a common labourer can afford it. The schoolmaster should be paid partly, but not entirely, by the public; for if he were paid wholly, or even mainly, by the public, he would soon learn to neglect his job. In Scotland, parish schools of this kind have taught almost all ordinary people to read, and a very large share of them to write and do arithmetic. In England, charity schools have had a similar effect, though not so widely, because they are not so widespread. If the books used in these little schools to teach reading were a little more instructive than they usually are, and if—instead of the smattering of Latin that the children of ordinary people are sometimes given there, which is almost never of any use to them—they were taught the basics of geometry and mechanics, then the formal education of this class of people would be about as complete as it could be. There is scarcely a common trade that does not offer some chance to apply the principles of geometry and mechanics, and that would not therefore gradually train and improve ordinary people in those principles, which are the necessary gateway to the most advanced as well as the most useful sciences.

The public can encourage people to acquire these most essential parts of an education by handing out small prizes and little badges of distinction to the children of ordinary people who excel at them.

The public can make almost the whole population acquire the most essential parts of an education by requiring every man to pass an exam or test in them before he can be admitted to the freedom of any guild, or be allowed to set up a trade in any village or chartered town.

This is exactly how the Greek and Roman republics kept their citizens fighting-fit: by making military and athletic training easy to get, by encouraging it, and even by requiring the whole population to learn it. They made the training easy to get by setting aside a particular place for learning and practising it, and by granting certain instructors the privilege of teaching there. These instructors do not seem to have had salaries or any exclusive privileges. Their whole reward came from what their pupils paid them, and a citizen who had learned his exercises in the public gymnasium had no legal advantage over one who had learned them privately, as long as the latter had learned them just as well. The republics encouraged people to take up these exercises by giving little prizes and badges of distinction to those who excelled. Winning a prize at the Olympic, Isthmian, or Nemean games brought glory not only to the winner himself but to his whole family and kin. And the duty every citizen was under to serve a set number of years in the republic's armies if called upon was enough by itself to make learning these exercises necessary, since without them he would not be fit for that service.

Modern Europe shows clearly enough that, as a society develops, the practice of military exercises gradually decays unless the government takes proper care to keep it up, and along with it the fighting spirit of the population at large. Yet the security of every society must always depend, more or less, on the fighting spirit of its people. Today, admittedly, that spirit alone, without the backing of a well-trained standing army, would probably not be enough to defend and secure any society. But where every citizen had a soldier's spirit, a smaller standing army would certainly do. That spirit would also greatly reduce the dangers to liberty—real or imagined—that people commonly fear from a standing army. Just as it would make the army far more effective against a foreign invader, so it would obstruct that army just as much if it were ever, unfortunately, turned against the country's own constitution.

The ancient institutions of Greece and Rome seem to have been far more effective at keeping up the population's fighting spirit than the modern arrangements we call militias. They were much simpler. Once set up, they ran themselves and needed little or no attention from government to keep them in full vigour. By contrast, keeping even a modern militia's complicated rules in tolerable working order takes constant and painful effort from the government; without it, they keep sliding into total neglect and disuse. The ancient institutions also reached far more people. Through them, the whole population was fully trained in the use of arms, whereas only a very small part of any people can ever be trained that way under a modern militia—except perhaps Switzerland's. But a coward, a man unable either to defend himself or to avenge himself, plainly lacks one of the most essential parts of a man's character. He is as crippled and deformed in mind as another man is in body who has lost some of his most essential limbs, or the use of them. He is plainly the more wretched and miserable of the two, because happiness and misery, which lie entirely in the mind, must depend more on whether the mind is healthy or sick, whole or maimed, than on the state of the body. Even if the people's fighting spirit were useless for defending society, preventing the mental crippling, deformity, and wretchedness that cowardice brings with it from spreading through the population would still deserve the most serious attention of government—in the same way that it would deserve serious attention to stop a leprosy, or any other loathsome and offensive disease, from spreading among them, even one that is neither deadly nor dangerous, where perhaps no other public good would come of such care besides preventing so great a public evil.

The same can be said of the gross ignorance and stupidity that, in a civilised society, seem so often to dull the minds of all the lower ranks of people. A man without the proper use of a man's intellectual faculties is, if anything, even more contemptible than a coward, and seems crippled and deformed in a still more essential part of human nature. Even if the state gained nothing from educating the lower ranks, it would still be worth its attention that they should not be left wholly untaught. But the state does in fact gain a good deal from their education. The better educated they are, the less prone they are to the delusions of fanaticism and superstition, which among ignorant nations so often cause the most dreadful upheavals. An educated and intelligent people are also always more decent and orderly than an ignorant and stupid one. Each of them feels more self-respect, and feels more likely to win the respect of his lawful superiors, and so is more inclined to respect those superiors. They are more inclined to examine, and more able to see through, the self-interested complaints of faction and sedition; and for that reason they are less easily misled into reckless or needless opposition to the government's measures. In free countries, where the safety of the government depends very much on how favourably the people judge its conduct, it must surely be of the highest importance that the people not be inclined to judge it rashly or on a whim.
Article III. The Cost of Institutions for Instructing People of All Ages

The institutions for instructing people of all ages are chiefly those for religious instruction. This kind of instruction aims not so much at making people good citizens in this world as at preparing them for another and better world in the life to come. The teachers of the doctrine that contains this instruction may, like other teachers, either depend entirely for their living on the voluntary contributions of their listeners, or draw it from some other fund that the law of their country may grant them—a landed estate, a tithe or land tax, an established salary or stipend. Their effort, zeal, and diligence are likely to be far greater in the first case than in the second. On this point, the teachers of a new religion have always had a considerable advantage when attacking the ancient established systems, whose clergy, resting comfortably on their endowments, had let the warmth of faith and devotion among the people grow cold, and, having given themselves up to laziness, had become wholly incapable of any vigorous effort even in defence of their own establishment. The clergy of an established and well-endowed religion often become learned and refined men, possessing all the virtues of gentlemen, or those qualities that can win the esteem of gentlemen; but they tend gradually to lose the qualities, both good and bad, that gave them authority and influence with the lower ranks of people, and that had perhaps been the original causes of their religion's success and establishment. Such a clergy, when attacked by a set of popular and bold—though perhaps stupid and ignorant—enthusiasts, find themselves as defenceless as the idle, soft, and well-fed nations of southern Asia were when the active, hardy, hungry Tartars of the north invaded them. In such an emergency, such a clergy usually have no other recourse than to call on the civil magistrate to persecute, destroy, or drive out their opponents as disturbers of the public peace. This is how the Roman Catholic clergy called on the magistrate to persecute the Protestants, and the Church of England to persecute the Dissenters; and how, in general, every religious sect, once it has enjoyed the security of a legal establishment for a century or two, has found itself unable to put up any vigorous defence against a new sect that chooses to attack its doctrine or discipline. On such occasions the advantage in learning and good writing may sometimes lie with the established church. But the arts of popularity, all the arts of gaining converts, are always on the side of its opponents. In England these arts have long been neglected by the well-endowed clergy of the established church, and are at present mainly practised by the Dissenters and the Methodists. The independent funding, however, that has in many places been arranged for Dissenting teachers through voluntary subscriptions, trusts, and other ways around the law, seems to have greatly cooled the zeal and energy of those teachers. Many of them have become very learned, clever, and respectable men, but in general they have stopped being very popular preachers. The Methodists, with not half the learning of the Dissenters, are far more in fashion.

In the Church of Rome the diligence and zeal of the lower clergy are kept more alive by the powerful motive of self-interest than perhaps in any established Protestant church. Many of the parish clergy draw a very large part of their living from the people's voluntary offerings—a source of income that confession gives them many chances to increase. The mendicant orders draw their entire living from such offerings. With them it is as with the hussars and light infantry of some armies: no plunder, no pay. The parish clergy are like teachers whose reward depends partly on a salary and partly on the fees they collect from their pupils, and these fees must always depend, more or less, on their diligence and reputation. The mendicant orders are like teachers whose living depends entirely on their own diligence. They are therefore obliged to use every art that can stir the devotion of ordinary people. Machiavelli observed that the founding of the two great mendicant orders of St Dominic and St Francis revived the flagging faith and devotion of the Catholic church in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. In Roman Catholic countries the spirit of devotion is kept up entirely by the monks and by the poorer parish clergy. The great dignitaries of the church, with all the polish of gentlemen and men of the world, and sometimes of learned men too, take care to maintain the necessary discipline over their inferiors, but seldom trouble themselves about instructing the people.

"Most of the trades and professions in a state," says by far the most distinguished philosopher and historian of our age, "are of such a kind that, while they serve the interests of society, they are also useful or agreeable to particular individuals; and in that case the magistrate's constant rule—except perhaps when an art is first introduced—is to leave the profession to itself and trust its support to the individuals who profit from it. The craftsmen, seeing their profits rise through their customers' favour, increase their skill and diligence as much as they can; and, since nothing is disturbed by ill-judged meddling, the supply of the goods is always sure to be kept fairly close to the demand.

"But there are also some occupations that, though useful and even necessary to a state, bring no profit or pleasure to any individual; and the supreme power must change its approach toward those who follow such professions. It must give them public support so they can make a living, and it must guard against the negligence to which they will naturally be prone—either by attaching particular honours to the profession, by setting up a long ladder of ranks and strict dependence, or by some other device. The people employed in finance, the navy, and the courts are examples of this kind.

"At first sight it might naturally be supposed that the clergy belong to the first class, and that their support, like that of lawyers and physicians, can safely be left to the generosity of the individuals who are attached to their teachings and who find benefit or comfort in their spiritual ministry and help. Their diligence and watchfulness will, no doubt, be sharpened by such an added motive, and their skill in the profession, as well as their knack for managing people's minds, must grow daily with their increasing practice, study, and attention.

"But if we look more closely, we shall find that this self-interested industry of the clergy is exactly what every wise lawgiver will try to prevent; because, in every religion but the true one, it is highly harmful, and it even has a natural tendency to pervert the truth by mixing into it a strong dose of superstition, folly, and delusion. Each spiritual operator, in order to make himself more precious and sacred in the eyes of his followers, will fill them with the most violent loathing of all other sects, and will keep trying, by some novelty, to rouse the flagging devotion of his audience. No regard will be paid to truth, morals, or decency in the doctrines he preaches. Every tenet will be adopted that best suits the disorderly passions of human nature. Customers will be drawn to each meeting-house by fresh effort and skill in playing on the passions and credulity of the populace. And in the end the magistrate will find that he has paid dearly for his intended thrift in saving the cost of a fixed establishment for the priests, and that in reality the most decent and advantageous arrangement he can make with these spiritual guides is to buy off their idleness by assigning them fixed salaries, so that there is no need for them to be active beyond merely keeping their flock from wandering off in search of new shepherds. And in this way religious establishments, though they usually arose at first from religious motives, turn out in the end to serve the political interests of society."

But whatever the good or bad effects of giving the clergy an independent income, it has perhaps very seldom been granted with those effects in view. Times of fierce religious controversy have generally been times of equally fierce political faction. On such occasions each political party has either found it, or imagined it, in its interest to ally itself with one or other of the rival religious sects. But this could only be done by adopting, or at least favouring, that particular sect's tenets. The sect lucky enough to be allied with the winning party naturally shared in its ally's victory, and through that ally's favour and protection was soon able, to some extent, to silence and crush all its rivals. Those rivals had generally allied themselves with the enemies of the winning party, and were therefore that party's enemies too. The clergy of this favoured sect, having thus become complete masters of the field, with their influence and authority over the people at its height, were powerful enough to overawe the chiefs and leaders of their own party and to force the magistrate to respect their views and wishes. Their first demand was usually that he silence and crush all their rivals; their second, that he grant them an independent income. Since they had generally done a good deal to win the victory, it seemed not unreasonable that they should have some share of the spoils. Besides, they were tired of pandering to the people and of depending on the public's whims for a living. So in making this demand they were consulting their own ease and comfort, without bothering about the effect it might have, in later times, on the influence and authority of their order. The magistrate, who could meet their demand only by handing over something he would much rather have taken or kept for himself, was seldom eager to grant it. But necessity always forced him to give in at last, though often only after many delays, evasions, and put-on excuses.

But if politics had never called religion to its aid—if the winning party, once victorious, had never adopted one sect's tenets over another's—it would probably have dealt with all the different sects equally and impartially, and let every man choose his own priest and his own religion as he saw fit. In that case there would no doubt have been a great many religious sects. Almost every congregation might have had a little sect of its own, or held some peculiar tenets of its own. Each teacher would no doubt have felt obliged to make every effort, and use every art, both to keep and to increase his number of followers. But since every other teacher would have felt the same pressure, no single teacher, or group of teachers, could have grown very powerful. The self-interested, active zeal of religious teachers can be dangerous and troublesome only where there is just one sect tolerated in society, or where a large society is split into two or three great sects whose teachers act in concert under a regular discipline and hierarchy. But that zeal must be entirely harmless where society is split into two or three hundred—or perhaps as many thousand—small sects, none of them large enough to disturb the public peace. The teachers of each sect, finding themselves surrounded on all sides by more enemies than friends, would be forced to learn the candour and moderation so rarely found among the teachers of those great sects whose tenets, backed by the magistrate, are held in reverence by almost everyone across vast kingdoms and empires, and who therefore see nothing around them but followers, disciples, and humble admirers. The teachers of each little sect, finding themselves almost alone, would be obliged to respect those of almost every other sect; and the concessions they would find it both convenient and agreeable to make to one another might in time probably reduce the doctrine of most of them to that pure and rational religion, free of every trace of absurdity, fraud, or fanaticism, which wise men in all ages have wished to see established—but which positive law has perhaps never yet established, and probably never will establish in any country, because where religion is concerned positive law always has been, and probably always will be, more or less swayed by popular superstition and enthusiasm. This plan of church government—or rather of no church government at all—was what the sect called the Independents (a sect, no doubt, of very wild enthusiasts) proposed to set up in England toward the end of the civil war. Had it been established, then, however unphilosophical its origin, it would probably by now have produced the most philosophical good temper and moderation toward every kind of religious belief. It has been established in Pennsylvania, where, although the Quakers happen to be the most numerous, the law in fact favours no one sect over another; and there, it is said, it has produced this philosophical good temper and moderation.

But even supposing this equal treatment did not produce such good temper and moderation in all, or even in most, of the religious sects of a particular country, still, provided those sects were numerous enough—and therefore each of them too small to disturb the public peace—each one's excessive zeal for its own tenets could hardly do much harm, and might on the contrary do several kinds of good. And if the government were firmly resolved both to leave them all alone and to make them all leave one another alone, there would be little danger that they would not, of their own accord, subdivide fast enough to soon become numerous enough.

In every civilised society—every society where the distinction of ranks has once been firmly established—there have always been two different schemes or systems of morality current at the same time. One may be called the strict or austere, the other the liberal or, if you like, the loose system. The first is generally admired and revered by ordinary people; the second is generally favoured and adopted by the so-called people of fashion. The main difference between these two opposing systems seems to lie in how severely they judge the vices of frivolity—the vices that tend to spring from great prosperity and from an excess of gaiety and good humour. In the liberal or loose system, luxury, reckless and even disorderly merriment, the pursuit of pleasure to some degree of excess, breaches of chastity (at least by one of the two sexes), and the like—provided they are not accompanied by gross indecency and do not lead to lying or injustice—are generally treated with a good deal of indulgence, and are easily excused or pardoned outright. In the austere system, by contrast, such excesses are regarded with the utmost loathing and disgust. The vices of frivolity are always ruinous to ordinary people, and a single week's carelessness and dissipation is often enough to ruin a poor workman for good, and to drive him, in despair, into committing the most enormous crimes. So the wiser and better sort of ordinary people have always had the utmost loathing and disgust for such excesses, which their experience tells them are so quickly fatal to people in their position. The disorder and extravagance of several years, on the other hand, will not always ruin a man of fashion; and people of that rank tend to regard the freedom to indulge in some degree of excess as one of the advantages of their wealth, and the liberty of doing so without censure or reproach as one of the privileges that belong to their station. So in people of their own rank they regard such excesses with only a slight degree of disapproval, and censure them either very mildly or not at all.

Almost all religious sects have begun among the common people, from whom they have generally drawn their earliest as well as their most numerous converts. The austere system of morality has therefore been adopted by these sects almost without exception—though there have been a few. It was the system by which they could best recommend themselves to that class of people, to whom they first proposed their plan of reform on what had been established before. Many of them, perhaps most of them, have even tried to gain credit by refining on this austere system and carrying it to some degree of folly and extravagance; and this excessive strictness has often done more than anything else to win them the respect and reverence of ordinary people.

A man of rank and fortune is, by his station, a prominent member of a great society that watches every part of his conduct, and so obliges him to watch it himself. His authority and standing depend very much on the respect this society pays him. He dares do nothing that would disgrace or discredit him in it, and so he is bound to observe very strictly whichever code of morals—liberal or austere—that the general consent of this society lays down for people of his rank and fortune. A man of low condition, by contrast, is far from being a prominent member of any great society. While he stays in a country village, his conduct may be noticed, and he may be obliged to mind it himself. In this situation, and only in this situation, he has what is called a character to lose. But as soon as he comes into a great city, he sinks into obscurity and darkness. Nobody observes or attends to his conduct, and so he is very likely to neglect it himself and abandon himself to every kind of low profligacy and vice. He never escapes this obscurity so effectively—his conduct never draws the attention of any respectable society so much—as by joining a small religious sect. From that moment he gains a standing he never had before. All his fellow sectaries, for the credit of the sect, have an interest in watching his conduct; and if he gives any occasion for scandal, if he strays far from the austere morals they almost always demand of one another, they punish him with what is always a very severe punishment, even where it does no real harm: expulsion or excommunication from the sect. Accordingly, in little religious sects the morals of ordinary people have almost always been remarkably regular and orderly—generally much more so than in the established church. Indeed, the morals of these little sects have often been disagreeably strict and unsociable.

There are, however, two very easy and effective remedies whose combined operation might let the state correct, without any force, whatever was unsociable or disagreeably strict in the morals of all the little sects into which the country was divided.

The first of these remedies is the study of science and philosophy, which the state could make almost universal among all people of middling or more than middling rank and fortune—not by giving salaries to teachers and so making them careless and idle, but by setting up some kind of examination, even in the higher and more difficult sciences, to be passed by everyone before he was allowed to practise any liberal profession, or to stand as a candidate for any honourable office of trust or profit. If the state laid on this class of men the necessity of learning, it would have no need to trouble itself about providing them with proper teachers. They would soon find better teachers for themselves than any the state could provide. Science is the great antidote to the poison of fanaticism and superstition; and where all the higher ranks of people were protected from it, the lower ranks could not be much exposed to it.

The second of these remedies is frequent and cheerful public entertainment. By encouraging—that is, by giving complete freedom to—all those who, out of their own interest, would try, without scandal or indecency, to amuse and divert the people through painting, poetry, music, dancing, and all sorts of dramatic shows and exhibitions, the state would easily dispel in most of them that melancholy, gloomy mood which is almost always the nurse of popular superstition and fanaticism. Public entertainments have always been dreaded and hated by all the fanatical promoters of these popular frenzies. The gaiety and good humour that such entertainments inspire were utterly at odds with the frame of mind best suited to those promoters' purposes, or that they could best work upon. Dramatic performances, besides, by often exposing their tricks to public ridicule, and sometimes even to public curses, were for that reason hated by them more than any other entertainment.

In a country where the law favoured the teachers of no one religion over another, none of them would need to have any particular or direct dependence on the sovereign or the executive power, nor would he need to have any hand in appointing or dismissing them from their posts. In such a situation the sovereign would have no reason to concern himself with them, beyond keeping the peace among them, just as among the rest of his subjects—that is, stopping them from persecuting, abusing, or oppressing one another. But it is quite otherwise in countries with an established or governing religion. There the sovereign can never be secure unless he has the means of influencing, to a considerable degree, most of the teachers of that religion.

The clergy of every established church form one great corporate body. They can act in concert and pursue their interest on a single plan and with one spirit, as fully as if they were directed by one man—and they often are under such direction. Their interest as a corporate body is never the same as the sovereign's, and is sometimes directly opposed to it. Their great interest is to keep up their authority with the people, and this authority rests on the supposed certainty and importance of the whole doctrine they preach, and on the supposed necessity of accepting every part of it with the most implicit faith in order to avoid eternal damnation. Should the sovereign be so rash as to seem to mock, or even to doubt himself, the most trifling part of their doctrine, or, out of humanity, to try to protect those who did either, the touchy pride of a clergy who depend on him in no way is at once roused to denounce him as a profane person, and to use all the terrors of religion to make the people transfer their allegiance to some more orthodox and obedient prince. Should he oppose any of their claims or encroachments, the danger is just as great. The princes who have dared in this way to rebel against the church have, on top of this crime of rebellion, generally been charged with the further crime of heresy, despite their solemn protestations of faith and humble submission to every tenet she chose to prescribe to them. But the authority of religion is greater than any other authority. The fears it stirs up overcome all other fears. When the authorised teachers of religion spread through the population doctrines that undermine the sovereign's authority, it is by force alone, or by the strength of a standing army, that he can maintain it. And even a standing army cannot give him any lasting security in this case; for if the soldiers are not foreigners—which can seldom be so—but drawn from the population, which must almost always be so, they are likely to be soon corrupted by those very doctrines. The revolutions that the turbulence of the Greek clergy kept stirring up in Constantinople as long as the Eastern Empire lasted, and the upheavals that, over several centuries, the turbulence of the Roman clergy kept stirring up in every part of Europe, show clearly enough how precarious and insecure the position of a sovereign must always be when he has no proper means of influencing the clergy of the established and governing religion of his country.

It is clear enough that articles of faith, like all other spiritual matters, do not properly fall within a temporal sovereign's department. Though he may be very well qualified to protect the people, he is seldom supposed to be qualified to instruct them. In such matters, therefore, his authority can seldom be enough to outweigh the united authority of the clergy of the established church. Yet the public peace, and his own security, may often depend on what doctrines they choose to spread about such matters. Since he can seldom directly oppose their decision with proper weight and authority, he must be able to influence it; and he can influence it only through the fears and hopes he can stir up in most members of the order. Those fears and hopes may consist in the fear of being deprived of office or otherwise punished, and the hope of further promotion.

In all Christian churches the clergy's benefices are a kind of freehold, which they hold not at someone's pleasure but for life or during good behaviour. If they held them on a more precarious footing, liable to be turned out at every slight annoyance to the sovereign or his ministers, it might be impossible for them to keep their authority with the people, who would then regard them as mercenary hangers-on of the court, in the sincerity of whose teaching they could no longer have any confidence. But should the sovereign try, in an irregular and violent way, to deprive any number of clergymen of their freeholds—perhaps because they had spread some factious or seditious doctrine with more than usual zeal—such persecution would only make both them and their doctrine ten times more popular, and so ten times more troublesome and dangerous, than they had been before. Fear is in almost every case a wretched instrument of government, and ought in particular never to be used against any order of men who have the slightest claim to independence. Trying to terrify them only irritates their bad temper and confirms them in an opposition that gentler treatment might perhaps easily induce them either to soften or to drop altogether. The violence the French government usually used to force all its parlements, or sovereign courts of justice, to register an unpopular edict very seldom succeeded. The means commonly used—imprisoning all the defiant members—one would think forcible enough. The princes of the house of Stuart sometimes used similar means to influence some members of the English Parliament, and generally found them just as stubborn. The English Parliament is now managed in another way; and a very small experiment that the Duke of Choiseul made about twelve years ago on the Parlement of Paris showed clearly enough that all the parlements of France might have been managed still more easily in the same way. That experiment was not pursued. For although management and persuasion are always the easiest and safest instruments of government, while force and violence are the worst and most dangerous, yet such, it seems, is man's natural insolence that he almost always disdains to use the good instrument except when he cannot or dare not use the bad one. The French government could and dared to use force, and therefore disdained to use management and persuasion. But there is no order of men, I believe, on whom it is so dangerous—so utterly ruinous—to use force and violence, as the experience of all ages shows, as the respected clergy of an established church. The rights, the privileges, the personal liberty of every individual clergyman who is on good terms with his own order are, even in the most despotic governments, more respected than those of any other person of nearly equal rank and fortune. This holds at every level of despotism, from the gentle and mild government of Paris to the violent and furious government of Constantinople. But though this order of men can scarcely ever be forced, they may be managed as easily as any other; and the security of the sovereign, as well as the public peace, seems to depend very much on his means of managing them—and those means seem to consist entirely in the preferment he has to bestow on them.

In the ancient constitution of the Christian church, the bishop of each diocese was chosen by the joint votes of the clergy and the people of the cathedral city. The people did not keep their right of election for long, and while they kept it they almost always acted under the clergy's influence, since in such spiritual matters the clergy seemed to be their natural guides. The clergy, however, soon grew tired of the trouble of managing them, and found it easier to elect their own bishops themselves. The abbot, likewise, was chosen by the monks of the monastery, at least in most abbeys. All the lower church benefices within the diocese were filled by the bishop, who gave them to whichever clergymen he saw fit. In this way all church preferments were at the church's disposal. The sovereign, though he might have some indirect influence over these elections, and though it was sometimes customary to ask both his consent to hold the election and his approval of the man chosen, had no direct or sufficient means of managing the clergy. Every clergyman's ambition naturally led him to court not so much his sovereign as his own order, from which alone he could hope for preferment.

Throughout most of Europe the pope gradually drew to himself, first the filling of almost all bishoprics and abbeys, or what were called the consistorial benefices, and afterwards, by various schemes and pretexts, of most of the lower benefices within each diocese—leaving the bishop little more than what was barely enough to give him a decent authority over his own clergy. By this arrangement the sovereign's position was made even worse than before. The clergy of all the different countries of Europe were thus formed into a kind of spiritual army, scattered in different quarters it is true, but whose every move and operation could now be directed by one head and conducted on one uniform plan. The clergy of each particular country could be regarded as a particular detachment of that army, whose operations could easily be supported and backed by all the other detachments stationed in the surrounding countries. Each detachment was not only independent of the sovereign of the country where it was stationed, and by which it was maintained, but dependent on a foreign sovereign who could at any time turn its weapons against the sovereign of that particular country, and back them with the weapons of all the other detachments.

Those weapons were about the most formidable imaginable. In the early state of Europe, before arts and manufactures had developed, the clergy's wealth gave them the same kind of influence over ordinary people that the great barons' wealth gave them over their vassals, tenants, and retainers. On the great landed estates that the misguided piety of both princes and private persons had bestowed on the church, jurisdictions were set up just like those of the great barons, and for the same reason. On these great estates the clergy, or their bailiffs, could easily keep the peace without help from the king or anyone else; and neither the king nor anyone else could keep the peace there without the clergy's help. So the clergy's jurisdictions in their particular baronies or manors were just as independent of the king's courts, and excluded their authority just as much, as those of the great temporal lords. The clergy's tenants, like those of the great barons, were almost all tenants at will, wholly dependent on their immediate lords, and so liable to be called out at pleasure to fight in any quarrel the clergy chose to take up. On top of the rents of these estates, the clergy held in the tithes a very large share of the rents of all the other estates in every kingdom of Europe. The revenues from both kinds of rent were mostly paid in kind—in corn, wine, cattle, poultry, and so on.
