The amount greatly exceeded what the clergy could consume themselves, and there were neither arts nor manufactures whose products they could trade the surplus for. The clergy could profit from this huge surplus only by spending it, as the great barons spent their own surplus revenues, on the most lavish hospitality and the most extensive charity. Both the hospitality and the charity of the ancient clergy are accordingly said to have been very great. They not only kept almost all the poor of every kingdom, but many knights and gentlemen often had no other means of living than to travel from monastery to monastery, on the pretext of devotion but really to enjoy the clergy's hospitality. The retainers of some particular prelates were often as numerous as those of the greatest lay lords, and the retainers of all the clergy together were perhaps more numerous than those of all the lay lords. There was always far more unity among the clergy than among the lay lords. The clergy were under a regular discipline and subordination to the papal authority. The lay lords were under no regular discipline or subordination, but almost always equally jealous of one another and of the king. So even if the tenants and retainers of the clergy together had been fewer than those of the great lay lords—and their tenants probably were much fewer—their unity would still have made them more formidable. The hospitality and charity of the clergy not only gave them command of a great worldly force but also greatly increased the weight of their spiritual weapons. Those virtues won them the highest respect and reverence among all the lower ranks of people, many of whom were constantly, and almost all of whom were occasionally, fed by them. Everything belonging or related to so popular an order—its possessions, its privileges, its doctrines—inevitably seemed sacred in the eyes of ordinary people, and every violation of them, whether real or alleged, the highest act of sacrilegious wickedness and profanity. In this state of things, if the sovereign often found it hard to resist a league of even a few of the great nobility, we cannot wonder that he found it still harder to resist the united force of the clergy of his own dominions, backed by that of the clergy of all the neighbouring dominions. In such circumstances, the wonder is not that he was sometimes forced to give in, but that he ever managed to resist at all.

The privileges the clergy enjoyed in those ancient times—which to us, living now, seem utterly absurd—such as their total exemption from secular jurisdiction, or what in England was called benefit of clergy, were the natural, or rather the necessary, consequences of this state of things. How dangerous it must have been for the sovereign to try to punish a clergyman for any crime whatever, if his order was disposed to protect him and to claim either that the evidence was too weak to convict so holy a man, or that the punishment was too severe to inflict on one whose person religion had made sacred! In such circumstances the sovereign could do no better than leave him to be tried by the ecclesiastical courts, who, for the honour of their own order, had an interest in restraining every member of it as much as possible from committing terrible crimes, or even from giving such gross scandal as might disgust the people.

In the state of things that prevailed through most of Europe during the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries, and for some time both before and after, the constitution of the Church of Rome may be regarded as the most formidable combination ever formed against the authority and security of civil government, as well as against the liberty, reason, and happiness of mankind, which can flourish only where civil government is able to protect them. In that constitution, the grossest delusions of superstition were upheld by the private interests of so great a number of people that they were put beyond all danger from any assault of human reason; for although human reason might perhaps have unveiled, even to ordinary people, some of the delusions of superstition, it could never have dissolved the ties of private interest. Had this constitution been attacked by no enemy but the feeble efforts of human reason, it would have lasted forever. But that immense, well-built structure, which all the wisdom and virtue of man could never have shaken, much less overturned, was, by the natural course of things, first weakened and afterwards partly destroyed; and it is now likely, in the course of a few more centuries perhaps, to crumble into ruins altogether.

The gradual progress of arts, manufactures, and commerce—the very causes that destroyed the power of the great barons—destroyed in the same way, through most of Europe, the whole worldly power of the clergy. In the products of arts, manufactures, and commerce the clergy, like the great barons, found something to trade their raw produce for, and so found a way to spend their entire revenues on themselves, without giving any considerable share to other people. Their charity gradually grew less extensive, their hospitality less generous, or less lavish. Their retainers consequently grew fewer, and by degrees dwindled away altogether. The clergy, too, like the great barons, wanted to get a better rent from their landed estates in order to spend it the same way, on gratifying their own private vanity and folly. But this increase of rent could be had only by granting leases to their tenants, who thereby became largely independent of them. So the ties of interest that had bound the lower ranks of people to the clergy were gradually broken and dissolved. They were even broken and dissolved sooner than those that bound the same ranks to the great barons; because the church's benefices, being mostly much smaller than the estates of the great barons, allowed the holder of each benefice to spend his whole revenue on himself much sooner. During most of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the power of the great barons was, throughout most of Europe, in full vigour. But the worldly power of the clergy, the absolute command they had once held over the population, was very much decayed. By that time the power of the church had been reduced, through most of Europe, very nearly to what came from its spiritual authority alone; and even that spiritual authority was much weakened once it was no longer backed by the charity and hospitality of the clergy. The lower ranks of people no longer looked on that order as they had before, as the comforters of their distress and the relievers of their poverty. On the contrary, they were provoked and disgusted by the vanity, luxury, and expense of the richer clergy, who seemed to be spending on their own pleasures what had always before been regarded as the patrimony of the poor.

In this state of things, the sovereigns in the different states of Europe tried to recover the influence they had once had over the disposal of the church's great benefices, by restoring to the deans and chapters of each diocese their ancient right of electing the bishop, and to the monks of each abbey that of electing the abbot. Re-establishing this ancient order was the aim of several statutes passed in England during the fourteenth century, notably what is called the Statute of Provisors, and of the Pragmatic Sanction established in France in the fifteenth century. For the election to be valid, the sovereign had both to consent to it beforehand and to approve the person chosen afterwards; and though the election was still supposed to be free, he nonetheless had all the indirect means his position naturally gave him of influencing the clergy in his own dominions. Other regulations of a similar tendency were set up in other parts of Europe. But the pope's power to fill the great benefices of the church seems, before the Reformation, to have been nowhere so effectively and universally restrained as in France and England. The Concordat afterwards, in the sixteenth century, gave the kings of France the absolute right of presenting to all the great, or so-called consistorial, benefices of the Gallican church.

Since the establishment of the Pragmatic Sanction and the Concordat, the clergy of France have generally shown less respect for the decrees of the papal court than the clergy of any other Catholic country. In all the disputes their sovereign has had with the pope, they have almost always sided with the sovereign. This independence of the French clergy from the court of Rome seems to rest chiefly on the Pragmatic Sanction and the Concordat. In the earlier periods of the monarchy, the French clergy appear to have been as devoted to the pope as those of any other country. When Robert, the second prince of the Capetian line, was most unjustly excommunicated by the court of Rome, his own servants, it is said, threw the food that came from his table to the dogs, and refused to taste anything themselves that had been polluted by the touch of a man in his situation. They were taught to do this, we may safely assume, by the clergy of his own dominions.

The claim of filling the great benefices of the church—a claim in whose defence the court of Rome had often shaken, and sometimes overturned, the thrones of some of the greatest sovereigns in Christendom—was in this way either restrained, or modified, or given up altogether in many different parts of Europe, even before the Reformation. As the clergy now had less influence over the people, so the state had more influence over the clergy. The clergy therefore had both less power and less inclination to disturb the state.

The authority of the Church of Rome was in this state of decline when the disputes that gave birth to the Reformation began in Germany and soon spread through every part of Europe. The new doctrines were everywhere received with great popular favour. They were spread with all the enthusiastic zeal that commonly fires the spirit of party when it attacks established authority. The teachers of these doctrines, though perhaps in other respects no more learned than many of the divines who defended the established church, seem in general to have known ecclesiastical history better, and to have understood the origin and growth of the system of beliefs on which the church's authority was founded; and this gave them the advantage in almost every dispute. The austerity of their manners gave them authority with ordinary people, who contrasted the strict regularity of their conduct with the disorderly lives of most of their own clergy. They also possessed, far more than their opponents, all the arts of popularity and of winning converts—arts that the lofty and dignified sons of the church had long neglected as being, to them, largely useless. The reasoning behind the new doctrines recommended them to some, their novelty to many, and hatred and contempt for the established clergy to a still greater number; but the zealous, passionate, fanatical, though often coarse and rustic eloquence with which they were preached almost everywhere recommended them to by far the greatest number of all.

The new doctrines succeeded so well almost everywhere that the princes who happened at the time to be on bad terms with the court of Rome were, by means of them, easily able to overturn the church in their own dominions, which, having lost the respect and reverence of the lower ranks of people, could put up scarcely any resistance. The court of Rome had offended some of the smaller princes in northern Germany, whom it had probably thought too insignificant to be worth humouring. So they all, without exception, established the Reformation in their dominions. The tyranny of Christian II and of Troll, archbishop of Uppsala, enabled Gustavus Vasa to drive them both out of Sweden. The pope favoured the tyrant and the archbishop, and Gustavus Vasa found no difficulty in establishing the Reformation in Sweden. Christian II was afterwards deposed from the throne of Denmark, where his conduct had made him as hated as in Sweden. The pope, however, was still inclined to favour him; and Frederick of Holstein, who had taken the throne in his place, took his revenge by following Gustavus Vasa's example. The magistrates of Berne and Zurich, who had no particular quarrel with the pope, established the Reformation with great ease in their respective cantons, where just beforehand some of the clergy had, by an imposture rather grosser than usual, made the whole order both hateful and contemptible.

In this critical state of its affairs, the papal court took considerable pains to cultivate the friendship of the powerful sovereigns of France and Spain, the latter of whom was at that time emperor of Germany. With their help it managed, though not without great difficulty and much bloodshed, either to suppress the Reformation altogether or to obstruct its progress greatly in their dominions. It was also quite willing to oblige the king of England. But given the circumstances of the time, it could not do so without offending a still greater sovereign, Charles V, king of Spain and emperor of Germany. Henry VIII, accordingly, though he did not himself embrace most of the doctrines of the Reformation, was nevertheless able, thanks to their general spread, to suppress all the monasteries and to abolish the authority of the Church of Rome in his dominions. That he went so far, even though he went no further, gave some satisfaction to the supporters of the Reformation, who, having gained control of the government in the reign of his son and successor, completed without any difficulty the work Henry VIII had begun.

In some countries, such as Scotland, where the government was weak, unpopular, and not very firmly established, the Reformation was strong enough to overturn not only the church but the state as well, for trying to support the church.

Among the followers of the Reformation scattered across the different countries of Europe, there was no general tribunal that, like the court of Rome or an ecumenical council, could settle all disputes among them and, with irresistible authority, lay down for all of them the exact limits of orthodoxy. So when the followers of the Reformation in one country happened to differ from their brethren in another, having no common judge to appeal to, the dispute could never be settled; and many such disputes arose among them. Those concerning the government of the church and the right of conferring church benefices were perhaps the most important to the peace and welfare of civil society. They gave rise, accordingly, to the two principal parties or sects among the followers of the Reformation—the Lutheran and the Calvinist—the only sects among them whose doctrine and discipline have ever yet been established by law in any part of Europe.

The followers of Luther, together with what is called the Church of England, kept more or less of episcopal government, maintained a hierarchy among the clergy, gave the sovereign the disposal of all the bishoprics and other consistorial benefices in his dominions, and thereby made him the real head of the church; and without depriving the bishop of the right of filling the smaller benefices in his diocese, they admitted and even favoured, for those benefices too, the right of presentation by the sovereign and by all other lay patrons. This system of church government was from the start favourable to peace and good order and to submission to the civil sovereign. It has accordingly never been the occasion of any tumult or civil disturbance in any country where it has once been established. The Church of England in particular has always prided herself, with good reason, on the unimpeachable loyalty of her principles. Under such a government, the clergy naturally try to recommend themselves to the sovereign, the court, and the nobility and gentry of the country, through whose influence they chiefly expect to obtain preferment. They court these patrons sometimes, no doubt, by the basest flattery and toadying, but often, too, by cultivating all those arts that best deserve, and are therefore most likely to win them, the esteem of people of rank and fortune: by their knowledge in all the different branches of useful and ornamental learning, by the decent generosity of their manners, by the sociable good humour of their conversation, and by their avowed contempt for those absurd and hypocritical austerities that fanatics preach and pretend to practise in order to draw on themselves the reverence, and on most men of rank and fortune (who openly admit they do not practise them) the abhorrence, of ordinary people. Such a clergy, however, while they court the higher ranks in this way, are very apt to neglect entirely the means of keeping up their influence and authority with the lower ones. They are listened to, esteemed, and respected by their superiors; but in front of their inferiors they are often unable to defend, effectively and convincingly, their own sober and moderate doctrines against the most ignorant enthusiast who chooses to attack them.

The followers of Zwingli, or more properly those of Calvin, on the contrary, gave the people of each parish the right of electing their own pastor whenever the church became vacant, and at the same time established the most perfect equality among the clergy. The first part of this arrangement, as long as it remained in force, seems to have produced nothing but disorder and confusion, and to have tended equally to corrupt the morals of both the clergy and the people. The second part seems never to have had any effects but thoroughly agreeable ones.

As long as the people of each parish kept the right of electing their own pastors, they almost always acted under the clergy's influence, and generally that of the most factious and fanatical members of the order. The clergy, in order to keep their influence in those popular elections, became—or pretended to become—many of them fanatics themselves, encouraged fanaticism among the people, and almost always gave the preference to the most fanatical candidate. So small a matter as the appointment of a parish priest almost always caused a violent contest, not only in one parish but in all the neighbouring ones, which seldom failed to take part in the quarrel. When the parish happened to lie in a great city, it split all the inhabitants into two parties; and when that city happened either to be a little republic in itself, or to be the head and capital of a little republic, as was the case with many of the considerable cities of Switzerland and Holland, every petty dispute of this kind, besides inflaming all their other rivalries, threatened to leave behind it both a new schism in the church and a new faction in the state. In those small republics, therefore, the magistrate very soon found it necessary, for the sake of keeping the public peace, to take to himself the right of presenting to all vacant benefices. In Scotland, the most extensive country in which this Presbyterian form of church government has ever been established, the rights of patronage were in effect abolished by the act that established Presbytery at the beginning of the reign of William III. That act at least gave certain classes of people in each parish the power to buy, for a very small price, the right of electing their own pastor. The arrangement this act set up was allowed to last about twenty-two years, but was abolished by the act of 10 Anne, ch. 12, on account of the confusion and disorder that this more popular mode of election had caused almost everywhere. In so extensive a country as Scotland, however, a disturbance in a remote parish was not as likely to trouble the government as in a smaller state. The act of 10 Anne restored the rights of patronage. But although in Scotland the law gives the benefice, without exception, to the person presented by the patron, the church nonetheless sometimes requires (for she has not been very consistent on this point) a certain concurrence of the people before she will grant the presentee what is called the cure of souls, or the ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the parish. At least she sometimes, out of an affected concern for the peace of the parish, delays the settlement until this concurrence can be obtained. The private meddling of some of the neighbouring clergy—sometimes to procure, but more often to prevent, this concurrence—and the popular arts they cultivate in order to meddle more effectively on such occasions, are perhaps the chief causes that keep alive whatever remains of the old fanatical spirit, in either the clergy or the people of Scotland.

The equality that the Presbyterian form of church government establishes among the clergy consists, first, in equality of authority or ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and second, in equality of income. In all Presbyterian churches the equality of authority is perfect; that of income is not. The difference between one benefice and another, however, is seldom large enough to tempt the holder of even a small one to court his patron by the base arts of flattery and toadying in order to get a better. In all the Presbyterian churches where the rights of patronage are thoroughly established, it is by nobler and better arts that the clergy in general try to win the favour of their superiors: by their learning, by the irreproachable regularity of their lives, and by the faithful and diligent discharge of their duty. Their patrons even often complain of the independence of their spirit, which they tend to construe as ingratitude for past favours, but which at worst is perhaps seldom more than the indifference that naturally arises from knowing that no further favours of the kind are ever to be expected. There is scarcely anywhere in Europe to be found a more learned, decent, independent, and respectable set of men than most of the Presbyterian clergy of Holland, Geneva, Switzerland, and Scotland.

Where church benefices are all nearly equal, none of them can be very great; and this moderation of income, though it can no doubt be carried too far, nonetheless has some very agreeable effects. Nothing but exemplary morals can give dignity to a man of small fortune. The vices of frivolity and vanity inevitably make him ridiculous, and are besides almost as ruinous to him as they are to ordinary people. In his own conduct, therefore, he is obliged to follow the system of morals that ordinary people most respect. He wins their esteem and affection by the very plan of life that his own interest and situation would lead him to follow. Ordinary people regard him with the kindness we naturally feel for one who comes close to our own condition but who, we think, ought to be in a higher one. Their kindness naturally calls forth his own. He grows careful to instruct them, and attentive to help and relieve them. He does not even despise the prejudices of people who are so disposed to be favourable to him, and never treats them with those contemptuous and arrogant airs we so often meet with in the proud dignitaries of rich and well-endowed churches. The Presbyterian clergy, accordingly, have more influence over the minds of ordinary people than perhaps the clergy of any other established church. And it is only in Presbyterian countries that we ever find ordinary people converted, without persecution, completely and almost to a man, to the established church.

In countries where most church benefices are very modest, a university chair is generally a better position than a church benefice. In that case the universities have the pick of all the churchmen of the country, who in every country make up by far the most numerous class of men of letters. Where many of the church benefices, on the contrary, are very considerable, the church naturally draws away from the universities most of their eminent men of letters, who generally find some patron who does himself credit by getting them church preferment. In the first case we are likely to find the universities filled with the most eminent men of letters in the country. In the second we are likely to find few eminent men among them, and those few among the youngest members of the body, who are likely, too, to be drained away from it before they can have gained enough experience and knowledge to be of much use to it. Voltaire notes that Father Porée, a Jesuit of no great standing in the republic of letters, was the only professor France ever had whose works were worth reading. In a country that has produced so many eminent men of letters, it must seem rather odd that scarcely one of them should have been a university professor. The famous Gassendi was, early in his life, a professor at the University of Aix. When his genius first began to show, it was pointed out to him that by going into the church he could easily find a much quieter and more comfortable living, as well as a better situation for pursuing his studies; and he at once took the advice. Voltaire's observation may, I believe, be applied not only to France but to all other Roman Catholic countries. We very rarely find in any of them an eminent man of letters who is a university professor, except perhaps in the professions of law and medicine, professions from which the church is not so likely to draw them away. After the Church of Rome, that of England is by far the richest and best-endowed church in Christendom. In England, accordingly, the church is continually draining the universities of all their best and ablest members; and an old college tutor known and distinguished across Europe as an eminent man of letters is as rarely to be found there as in any Roman Catholic country. In Geneva, on the contrary, in the Protestant cantons of Switzerland, in the Protestant countries of Germany, in Holland, in Scotland, in Sweden, and in Denmark, the most eminent men of letters those countries have produced have—not all, indeed, but the far greater part of them—been university professors. In those countries the universities are continually draining the church of all its most eminent men of letters.

It may perhaps be worth remarking that, if we leave out the poets, a few orators, and a few historians, by far the greater part of the other eminent men of letters of both Greece and Rome appear to have been either public or private teachers, generally either of philosophy or of rhetoric. This will be found to hold true from the days of Lysias and Isocrates, of Plato and Aristotle, down to those of Plutarch and Epictetus, Suetonius and Quintilian. To impose on a man the necessity of teaching, year after year, in some particular branch of science seems in fact to be the most effective method for making him completely master of it himself. By being obliged to go over the same ground every year, he necessarily becomes, in a few years, if he is good for anything, well acquainted with every part of it; and if on some particular point he has formed too hasty an opinion one year, when in the course of his lectures he comes to reconsider the same subject the next year, he is very likely to correct it. Just as being a teacher of science is the natural employment of a mere man of letters, so it is also perhaps the training most likely to make him a man of solid learning and knowledge. The moderation of church incomes naturally tends to draw most of the men of letters in a country to the employment in which they can be most useful to the public, and at the same time to give them the best education they are perhaps capable of receiving. It tends to make their learning both as solid and as useful as possible.

It ought to be noted that the revenue of every established church—except for whatever parts of it come from particular lands or manors—is a branch of the general revenue of the state, diverted here to a purpose very different from the defence of the state. The tithe, for example, is really a land tax, which makes it impossible for landowners to contribute as much toward the defence of the state as they otherwise could. Yet the rent of land is, according to some, the sole fund, and according to others the chief fund, from which in all great monarchies the needs of the state must ultimately be met. The more of this fund that is given to the church, the less, plainly, can be spared for the state. It may be laid down as a certain maxim that, all other things being equal, the richer the church, the poorer must necessarily be either the sovereign on the one hand or the people on the other; and in all cases the less able the state must be to defend itself. In several Protestant countries, particularly in all the Protestant cantons of Switzerland, the revenue that anciently belonged to the Roman Catholic church—the tithes and church lands—has proved a fund sufficient not only to provide adequate salaries for the established clergy but to meet, with little or no addition, all the other expenses of the state. The magistrates of the powerful canton of Berne in particular have, out of the savings from this fund, accumulated a very large sum, supposed to amount to several millions; part of it is kept in a public treasury, and part is lent out at interest in what are called the public funds of the various indebted nations of Europe, chiefly those of France and Great Britain. What the whole expense of the church—whether of Berne or of any other Protestant canton—costs the state, I do not pretend to know. By a very exact account it appears that in 1755 the whole revenue of the clergy of the Church of Scotland, including their glebe or church lands and the rent of their manses or dwelling-houses, valued at a reasonable estimate, amounted to only £68,514 1s. 5¹⁄₁₂d. This very moderate revenue affords a decent living to nine hundred and forty-four ministers. The whole expense of the church, including what is occasionally laid out for building and repairing churches and ministers' manses, cannot well be supposed to exceed eighty or eighty-five thousand pounds a year. The most opulent church in Christendom does not maintain better the uniformity of faith, the fervour of devotion, the spirit of order, regularity, and austere morals among the people than this very poorly endowed Church of Scotland. All the good effects, both civil and religious, that an established church can be supposed to produce are produced by it as fully as by any other. Most of the Protestant churches of Switzerland, which in general are no better endowed than the Church of Scotland, produce those effects to an even higher degree. In most of the Protestant cantons there is not a single person to be found who does not profess himself a member of the established church. If anyone professes himself of any other, indeed, the law obliges him to leave the canton. But so harsh, or rather so oppressive, a law could never have been carried out in such free countries had not the diligence of the clergy already converted the whole body of the people, with perhaps only a few individual exceptions, to the established church. In some parts of Switzerland, accordingly, where, owing to the accidental union of a Protestant and a Roman Catholic country, the conversion has not been so complete, both religions are not only tolerated but established by law.

The proper performance of every service seems to require that its pay or reward should be matched, as closely as possible, to the nature of the service. If a service is very much underpaid, it is very apt to suffer from the meanness and incapacity of most of those employed in it. If it is very much overpaid, it is apt to suffer, perhaps even more, from their negligence and idleness. A man of large income, whatever his profession, thinks he ought to live like other men of large income, and to spend a great part of his time in festivity, vanity, and dissipation. But in a clergyman this way of life not only consumes the time that ought to be spent on the duties of his office, but, in the eyes of ordinary people, almost entirely destroys that holiness of character which alone can enable him to perform those duties with proper weight and authority.
Part IV. The Cost of Supporting the Dignity of the Sovereign

Over and above the expenses needed to enable the sovereign to perform his various duties, a certain expense is required to support his dignity. This expense varies both with the different stages of a society's development and with its different forms of government.

In a wealthy and advanced society, where every different order of people is growing more lavish day by day in their houses, their furniture, their tables, their dress, and their carriages, it can hardly be expected that the sovereign alone should hold out against the fashion. He naturally, therefore—or rather necessarily—becomes more lavish in all these things too. His dignity even seems to require it.

Just as a monarch is, in point of dignity, raised further above his subjects than the chief magistrate of any republic is ever supposed to be above his fellow citizens, so a greater expense is needed to support that higher dignity. We naturally expect more splendour in a king's court than in the residence of a doge or a burgomaster.
Conclusion

The expense of defending society, and that of supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate, are both laid out for the general benefit of the whole society. It is reasonable, therefore, that they should be met by the general contribution of the whole society, with all the different members contributing as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities.

The expense of the administration of justice, too, may no doubt be regarded as laid out for the benefit of the whole society. There is therefore nothing improper in its being met by the general contribution of the whole society. The people, however, who give rise to this expense are those who, by their injustice of one kind or another, make it necessary to seek redress or protection from the courts of justice. And the people most directly benefited by this expense are those whom the courts either restore to their rights or maintain in them. The expense of administering justice may therefore very properly be met by the particular contribution of one or other, or both, of these two different sets of people, as different occasions may require—that is, by court fees. There is no need to resort to the general contribution of the whole society, except to convict those criminals who have no estate or fund of their own sufficient to pay those fees.

Those local or provincial expenses whose benefit is local or provincial—what is spent, for example, on the policing of a particular town or district—ought to be met by a local or provincial revenue, and ought to be no burden on the general revenue of society. It is unjust that the whole society should contribute toward an expense whose benefit is confined to a part of it.

The expense of maintaining good roads and communications is, no doubt, beneficial to the whole society, and may therefore, without any injustice, be met by the general contributions of the whole society. This expense, however, is most directly and immediately beneficial to those who travel or carry goods from one place to another, and to those who consume such goods. The turnpike tolls in England, and the duties called peages in other countries, lay it entirely on these two different sets of people, and thereby relieve the general revenue of society from a very considerable burden.

The expense of the institutions for education and religious instruction is likewise, no doubt, beneficial to the whole society, and may therefore, without injustice, be met by the general contribution of the whole society. This expense, however, might perhaps with equal propriety, and even with some advantage, be met entirely by those who receive the immediate benefit of such education and instruction, or by the voluntary contributions of those who think they have need of either.

When the institutions, or public works, that benefit the whole society either cannot be maintained entirely, or are not maintained entirely, by the contributions of those particular members of society who benefit most directly from them, the shortfall must in most cases be made up by the general contribution of the whole society. The general revenue of society, over and above meeting the expense of defending society and of supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate, must make up for the shortfall in many particular branches of revenue. The sources of this general or public revenue I shall try to explain in the following chapter.
